items.title: Over 50% of financial industry ready for data localisation — CBN
items.description: By Babajide Komolafe The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) yesterday said that more than 50 per cent of Nigeria’s financial industry is ready to comply with data localisation requirements, stressing that the country must strengthen its digital sovereignty without undermining innovation and global technology integration. The Director, Payment System Supervision Department, CBN, Dr. Rakyat Yusuf, disclosed this at the CBN-National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) Executive Regulatory Dialogue on the National Sovereign Cloud Initiative (NSCI) and data localisation in Lagos. Yusuf said a survey conducted by the apex bank showed that more than half of the industry was prepared to comply, expressing optimism that the remaining institutions would make progress following clarifications provided at the dialogue. “A survey we conducted to generate data on the level of preparedness has shown that more than 50 per cent of the industry is ready to comply,” she said. She added: “Ultimately, we expect everyone to be on board by January 2027 to ensure that payment data is properly localised.” According to her, the policy is about “our sovereignty, clarity and visibility over our transaction data,” as well as ensuring financial system stability.” Yusuf said the CBN’s priority was to support financial institutions in achieving compliance rather than resorting immediately to sanctions. “However, where we identify a deliberate attempt to avoid compliance, sanctions will come into play. There will be sanctions for non-compliance,” she warned. Also speaking, the Deputy Governor, Financial System Stability, CBN, Lamido Yuguda, said Nigeria must strengthen control over its critical digital infrastructure while remaining open to global technological developments. He said: “The objective of the National Sovereign Cloud Initiative should not be to constrain innovation or isolate Nigeria from global technological developments. Rather, it should provide the security, resilience, and regulatory certainty necessary to support investment, innovation, and sustainable growth.” Yuguda said the resilience of the financial system increasingly depended on the digital infrastructure supporting it. He added: “We must strengthen digital sovereignty while remaining globally competitive; enhance security without constraining innovation; and promote localisation while ensuring that the financial system continues to benefit from efficient and reliable technology.” Meanwhile, NITDA Director-General, Kashifu Abdullahi, assured financial institutions that Nigeria’s technology ecosystem had the capacity to support the implementation of the sovereign cloud initiative. “Today’s workshop is to give you the assurance that the technology exists, the Nigerian tech ecosystem is capable, and it can support you in complying with your regulator’s mandate or directive,” he said. Abdullahi said digital sovereignty was not about isolation or building every technology locally, but developing Nigeria’s capacity to compete globally and maintain control over critical infrastructure. “It is about building our digital capacity to compete in the world we are in today,” he said. He warned that external disruptions, including submarine cable outages and geopolitical crises, should not automatically affect Nigeria’s payment system. Abdullahi added that the initiative would provide financial institutions with greater choice of technology providers and help prevent dependence on a single vendor, country or technology platform. The post Over 50% of financial industry ready for data localisation — CBN appeared first on Vanguard News .

Hardship: Our problems with FG’s 90-day relief plan —Labour
items.description: By Victor Ahiuma-Young In an apparent response to growing public concern and outcry over the high cost of living and the worsening economic hardship confronting Nigerians, the Federal Government recently announced a 90-day relief plan aimed at providing succour to workers and the wider population. However, rather than inspire confidence, the initiative has come under intense scrutiny from the Nigeria Labour Congress, NLC, which questions its transparency, effectiveness and capacity to address the underlying causes of the crisis. The labour centre has described the intervention as a “confession, not a solution,” arguing that temporary palliatives cannot replace concrete measures to tackle rising living costs, declining purchasing power and widespread impoverishment. The NLC also demanded the disclosure of the details of the plan, alongside concrete action on wage awards, petroleum prices, tax relief and the review of the national minimum wage, arguing that Nigerians need practical solutions rather than another set of promises. In this interview with Vanguard, NLC Assistant General Secretary, Chris Onyeka, explains the labour movement’s reservations about the plan, outlines its demands for urgent economic relief and challenges the Federal Government to move beyond promises and implement sustainable solutions to the hardship facing Nigerian workers and the masses. Onyeka said: “Our response to the federal government’s so-called 90-day plan to ease the cost of living is unambiguous. This plan is not a remedy; it is a confession. It is the government’s tacit admission, finally dragged out of it by the sheer weight of popular suffering, that its policies of the past nearly four years have afflicted the Nigerian people rather than improved their lives. “For years, the government denied that its reforms were producing pain. Various Ministers told us there was no suffering while other official spokespeople insisted the economy was on the right track. Now, with the announcement of a 90-day cost-of-living plan, the government has conceded the obvious; something is deeply wrong, and it was caused by the very policies it once defended. “But a confession is not a cure and, a plan cobbled together in panic is not a plan for the people. It is perceptibly playing politics with the genuine cries of Nigerian workers and masses. ‘We haven’t seen the plan’ “The truth is that we have not seen the Plan neither have any citizen It claims to help. We know that the most basic demand of any democratic governance is transparency. Yet nobody; not us in the NLC, not civil society, not the Nigerian workers and masses facing the crisis of survival daily; has seen this 90-day plan or knows what it contains. Any genuine plan to reduce the suffering of Nigerian workers would be a welcome development. But it is our responsibility, as the organised voice of workers, to demand that the government put this plan on the table for all of us to see. “Have we not been here before? Just a few weeks ago, the federal government came up with a 30-day selected fuel discount that was clearly a panic measure that amounted to nothing. It did not work in any way to assuage the sufferings of the people as it was tokenism dressed up as policy. “We would have loved to have been hopeful but we regrettably have no reason to believe the 90-day plan is anything more than a repeat performance; another promise on paper designed to hoodwink Nigerian workers and masses, just like the schemes and promises that came before it. “In generating this plan, Government should be bold to tell Nigerians who it Consulted? That is the question the Government may not be able to answer. We must also ask; which stakeholders did the government consult before coming up with such a plan? Did it consult the trade union movement; the organised representatives of Nigerian workers? Did it consult the civil society organisations that represent the people it governs? “There is no workable solution that can proceed from a government whose policy measures of the last nearly four years have only caused humongous hardship among the citizenry. Effective and sustainable solutions can only be founded when government learns to engage the people in creative conversations. It is not when you sit down in the corridors of power and hand down schemes to the people, instead of allowing them to conceive, design and implement the projects and policies directed toward solving their own socioeconomic problems. “This top-down, elitist approach; the politics of imposition; is precisely why the policies fail. The people are treated as objects of policy rather than subjects of their own liberation. The 90 days are questionable days, designed once again to hoodwink Nigerian workers and masses for political gains. A palliative, not a solution “And we must ask the obvious question: even if whatever measures involved in the 90-day plan work, what happens to the people and workers after 90 days? A 90-day palliative is not a structural solution. It is a bandage on a wound that requires surgery. “The timing of this plan is deeply suspect; it reeks of political motivation, coming as it does ahead of the 2027 general elections cycle that begins in January 2027. This is not economic policy; it is electoral calculation dressed in the language of relief. “When we are therefore asked whether it does assuage our anger as NLC, we are compelled to retort that this is a question that misses the point. It is not right to talk about “NLC’s anger” because it never was. It is rather right to talk about the sufferings of Nigerian workers and masses so, the better question is: does this plan address the worries of the Nigerian people? It clearly does not as there are no signs on the ground since the pronouncement of the plans to demonstrate any serious implementation. “The NLC was never asking for tokenistic measures. We were asking for concrete actions that would ameliorate these sufferings. The situation clearly transcends feelings of anger; it is about the existential threats that confront every Nigerian daily as a result of the policies of government. “The government’s plan does not address these threats to the lives of Nigerian workers because there is no concrete and workable action around the so-called plan. Anger is a luxury of the comfortable; what Nigerian workers face is survival, and the government is offering them theatre. “Whether it meets our expectations deserves a very simple answer; No, because the basics are missing. The expectation of Nigerian workers and masses, as championed by the NLC, is that the yoke of hunger and impoverishment be lifted from off the shoulders of Nigerian workers and peoples. What we have received instead are just the usual promissory notes. “Specifically, where is the wage award to keep Nigerian workers and masses surviving until the next national minimum wage is implemented? Where is the reduction in the prices of petroleum products that would ease the cost of transportation around the country, thus reducing food inflation and the prices of other basic commodities? These are not radical demands; they are the minimum conditions for survival. The plan does not in any way meet our expectations as workers and as a people. “On whether it meets the demands of the NLC, it can be said that the Government decided to go fishing instead of embarking on providing clear-cut solutions. The so-called plan does not address the issue of kick-starting the process for a statutory review of the national minimum wage. “It does not speak to the demands of Joint Health Workers Union of Nigeria, JOHESU and Joint Public Service Negotiating Council, JPSNC. “It does not speak to tax relief for Nigerian workers and masses, which would help put more money in the pockets of Nigerian workers. Government is therefore fishing and not seriously interested in solving the problems raised by the NLC. “This is governance by gesture; a politics of appearance rather than substance, in which announcements substitute for action and the suffering of the masses becomes background noise to the business of power. “Asking about stopping a planned strike truly shows a deep misunderstanding of our struggle. The NLC did not say that it was going to embark on strike. It stated that it will take remedial actions if its demands were not met. However, the responses of government thus far are not the kind that brings comfort to the workers and masses. “Whether they are enough to stop workers and masses from embarking on actions that will compel government to act reasonably remains to be seen. Discussions at the level of the Federal Ministry of Labour with other officials; without enough mandates from other ministries; have only gone to show that the government is not paying serious attention to the cries of Nigerian workers and masses. If this continues, nobody can guarantee how Nigerian workers and masses will react in due course. Change economic policies “The larger truth is that we unfortunately operate a system that produces suffering by design because of our insistence on adhering hook, line and sinker to neo-liberal prescriptions. The NLC’s response to the 90-day plan must be understood in its broader context. “The government’s policies of the last nearly four years; the removal of fuel subsidies without corresponding relief, the floating of the Naira, the assault on real wages; have not been accidental errors. They are the predictable outcomes of a neo-liberal policy framework that prioritises fiscal consolidation and the demands of international creditors over the lives and dignity of Nigerian workers. “The 90-day plan is an attempt to manage the political consequences of this framework without changing the framework itself. It is crisis management for the ruling class, not liberation for the working class. “The NLC’s position is not ‘anger.’ It is a clear-eyed demand for a different path; one in which the people are not passive recipients of elite-designed schemes but active participants in the design and implementation of the policies that govern their lives. That is what creative conversation means “ That is what sustainable solutions require. Until the government abandons its top-down, ‘impositionary’ approach and sits with the organised representatives of the people to build a genuine programme of relief and reconstruction, the 90-day plan will remain what it appears to be; another questionable promise, another political manoeuvre, another missed opportunity to lift the yoke of hunger and impoverishment from the shoulders of Nigerian workers and masses. “The government has admitted its policies have afflicted the people. Now it must do more than announce a 90-day reprieve. It must change the policies. And it must do so with the people, not to them. Having shown humility by ceasing the denial of the existence of massive hunger and suffering, NLC expects the government to seek for the cocreation of policies and paths that would address these consequences now, short term and long term The post Hardship: Our problems with FG’s 90-day relief plan —Labour appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, October 29, 2026
items.description: Trading in Nigeria’s foreign exchange market opened on Thursday with the local currency displaying steady conditions against the United States dollar across both official and unofficial channels. At the official Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM), the Naira traded around N1,346.05 per US dollar. Spot market activity recorded moderate intra-day movements as commercial banks and corporate entities executed transactions for foreign trade, import bills, and capital remittances. The rate maintains a tight range following ongoing liquidity support and market interventions from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) aimed at easing demand pressure. In the parallel market, commonly referred to as the black market, street traders and Bureau De Change operators in major hubs including Lagos, Abuja, and Kano quoted buying rates around N1,375 per dollar, while selling rates floated near N1,385 per dollar. The parallel market premium remains relatively narrow compared to the official rate. Market analysts attribute the market stability to sustained external reserves, which hold above $55 billion. Strong foreign inflows from oil exports and diaspora remittances continue to support liquidity across both FX channels. Market participants expect trading conditions to remain stable as regular commercial order flows are absorbed throughout the business day. items.title: Bangladesh presses India before Ganges water treaty expires
items.description: With a 30-year Ganges water-sharing treaty with India expiring in December, Bangladesh fears failure to strike a new deal could deepen water shortages, threatening tens of millions of livelihoods. In Bangladesh’s parched Barind region, 72-year-old Bikash Soren remembers when the Ganges river flowing in from neighbouring India carried large boats past his village year-round. “For almost three months a year, you hardly see the river flowing,” the Protestant priest said. Two farmers died by suicide last season, he added, after dwindling water levels left their rice and wheat crops in tatters. Shrinking flows in the Ganges have also slashed fish catches in the river, known in Bangladesh as the Padma. “Where will we find fish now?” said Abu Bakar Siddique, 55, who has switched to fish farming in ponds. “I used to catch many kinds.” The 2,525-kilometre Ganges flows through the world’s most populous river basin, home to 655 million people including more than 50 million in Bangladesh, according to the World Bank. This aerial photograph taken on October 13, 2026 shows wetlands along the Padma river at Ramnathpur village, near the Bangladesh-India frontier in Bangladesh’s Rajshahi division. —AFP/File The 1996 treaty, which expires on December 12, governs dry-season water sharing at India’s Farakka Barrage, 20 kilometres upstream of Bangladesh. But Bangladesh needs a new deal based on “mutual benefit and respect”, Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, a prime ministerial adviser who heads a technical committee on water-sharing, told AFP . Water arguments over 54 cross-border rivers between India and Bangladesh stretch back decades, and the Ganges is among the most important. Malik Fida A. Khan, a former Bangladeshi member of the Joint Rivers Commission (JRC), the body overseeing water-sharing, said India had built “additional dams” upstream. “This time, the agreement must include provisions on climate change — and take the entire river basin into account,” he said. Soured relations Bangladesh said India had not responded to its request to negotiate a treaty renewal. New Delhi’s foreign ministry said that “discussions regarding river-related matters” are a matter for the JRC commission, which held its last technical talks back in May. The last officially confirmed ministerial-level JRC meeting was in 2022 — after a 12-year gap. And a proposed water-sharing deal for the cross-border Teesta river has been stalled since 2011. Relations between New Delhi and Dhaka have soured since Bangladesh’s ex-leader Sheikh Hasina fled to old ally India, where she remains, following a 2024 uprising. This aerial photograph taken on October 12, 2026 shows a settlement of climate-displaced people following the erosion of Padma river at Namo Jagannathpur village, near the Bangladesh-India frontier in Bangladesh’s Rajshahi division. —AFP/File Hasina, sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity, has vowed to return to Bangladesh from India in December, the month the treaty she signed expires. Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman may also reportedly visit India before the treaty expires, but no visit has been confirmed . Arguments date back to 1975, when India opened the 2.2-kilometre long Farakka Barrage. Bangladesh accused India of diverting most of the water. The United Nations intervened in the dispute and a deal was agreed in 1977. But water-sharing arrangements lapsed a decade later, bringing severe consequences, said Sheikh Rokon of Dhaka-based environmental group Riverine People. “The Ganges suffered during the years without a treaty, and at least three rivers almost dried up,” Rokon said. One was the Gorai, which carries freshwater into the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and a World Heritage site, helping limit saltwater intrusion as sea levels rise. Bangladesh’s Ganges-Kobadak Irrigation Project, designed to water 955 square kilometres of farmland, the country’s largest, “became inoperative because of water scarcity”, Rokon said. In May, Dhaka approved the Padma Barrage, a $2.8-billion project intended to ease shortages and include a 113-megawatt hydropower plant. ‘Disastrous’ The 1996 treaty has no automatic extension clause. “If we fail to reach a deal, I fear the situation will be worse than what we experienced during the years without a treaty,” Rokon added. “Demand for freshwater on both sides has increased significantly.” Even with the treaty in place, the Ganges-Kobadak project has shrunk to 550 square kilometres, according to Bangladeshi state news agency BSS . “If the river does not carry enough water, the consequences could be disastrous,” said Chowdhury Sarwar Jahan, a geology professor at Bangladesh’s University of Rajshahi. This photograph taken on October 13, 2026 shows a fisherman wading through the Padma river at Ramnathpur village, near the Bangladesh-India frontier in Bangladesh’s Rajshahi division. —AFP/File Bangladesh’s agriculture-dependent economy is already reeling from the impact of climate change, which compounds shifting river flows, alternating dry-season shortages and intense monsoon floods washing away farmland and villages. In Chapainawabganj district, the river has widened by three kilometres in recent years — nearly doubling its size — according to Bangladesh’s Water Development Board. Rehana Khatun, 50, described the “howling sound” as floods destroyed her home in Fielder Bazar village. “The river turned wild and started swallowing everything along the bank,” said Khatun, who now lives in a bamboo shelter. “And the trauma stays with children long after the waters recede.”

84.9m informal workers face retirement without safety net
items.description: By Victor Ahiuma-Young The National Pension Commission, PenCom, is stepping up efforts to expand pension coverage among Nigeria’s self-employed and informal sector workers, as an estimated 84.9 million people remain without pension coverage, exposing a significant gap in the country’s retirement security system. Figures presented at the 2026 Annual PenCom Media Conference in in Lagos, showed that although the informal sector accounts for an estimated 93 per cent of Nigeria’s workforce, only 242,690 informal sector workers had enrolled in the Personal Pension Plan, PPP, as of July 2026. The figures, based on estimates of the informal sector workforce, put pension coverage among the group at just 0.29 per cent, highlighting the challenge facing efforts to bring millions of traders, artisans, farmers, professionals and gig workers into the pension system. The Personal Pension Plan was introduced under Section 2(3) of the Pension Reform Act, PRA, 2014 to extend pension coverage to self-employed persons and workers in the informal sector who may not have access to conventional employer-sponsored retirement savings arrangements. The scheme allows eligible contributors to make flexible payments daily, weekly, monthly or at their convenience, depending on their income and circumstances. Registration requires a National Identification Number (NIN) and a phone number, while prospective contributors can register directly with a Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) or through an accredited pension agent. However, the presentation identified several obstacles to wider participation, including irregular earnings, limited awareness, distrust of financial institutions, preference for readily accessible savings, geographical barriers and gaps in digital literacy. For many informal sector workers, whose earnings may fluctuate considerably, setting aside money for retirement can be difficult when contributions compete with immediate household and business expenses The presentation also noted that access to a pension account does not necessarily translate into sustained savings, as some contributors may register without making regular or subsequent payments. It stressed that the success of the Personal Pension Plan should therefore be measured not only by the number of registered accounts but also by active contributors, frequency of contributions, consistency of saving, average account balances and the adequacy of retirement benefits. Under the Plan’s contribution structure, 50 per cent of contributions constitutes the contingent portion, which may be withdrawn three months after the initial contribution and subsequently once every two months. The remaining 50 per cent is designated for retirement benefits and is accessible from age 50, or earlier in cases of medical incapacitation, subject to applicable regulations To widen participation, PenCom has accredited pension agents to help bring the scheme closer to underserved communities and workers who may have limited access to conventional pension services. The agents are expected to facilitate enrolment, support contributions and account updates through approved channels, and conduct public sensitisation and financial literacy activities. Six approved pension agents were listed in the presentation as having received accreditation across three dates in 2026: Awabah Remit Services Limited in February; e-Tranzact International Limited and NextAutomate APA Limited in June; and SunTrust Bank Nigeria Limited, PrimeTrust APA Limited and Majestic APA Limited in September. The presentation further identified financial literacy, trust-building, convenient payment channels and contribution arrangements suited to irregular earnings as important areas for improving participation and encouraging long-term saving. It also highlighted the gender dimension of the challenge, citing an estimate that 96 per cent of employed women work in the informal sector, making the expansion of pension coverage particularly relevant to women whose livelihoods fall outside formal employment arrangements. Beyond increasing enrolment, the commission’s challenge is to ensure that workers remain active contributors and accumulate sufficient savings to support them in retirement. The presentation concluded that expanding access alone would not close Nigeria’s pension gap. Sustained participation, consistent contributions and adequate retirement balances are essential to turning the Personal Pension Plan into a meaningful source of financial security for the country’s vast informal workforce. The post 84.9m informal workers face retirement without safety net appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: At least 5 killed, over two dozen injured as bus plunges into drain in Punjab's Hafizabad
items.description: LAHORE: At least five people were killed and 27 others injured when a passenger bus plunged into a drain in Punjab’s Hafizabad district on Thursday, according to Rescue 1122. Rescue services said the mishap occurred in the Fatehke area of Pindi Bhattian tehsil. The bus was reportedly on its way from Raiwind to Chiniot. According to rescue officials, overspeeding caused the driver to lose control of the vehicle. Soon after the accident, teams from Rescue 1122 reached the site and launched rescue operations. The injured were provided with first aid at the scene while 20 of them were also taken to hospital, Rescue 1122 said. With the assistance of the local government, a crane was used to lift the bus, after which the bodies of five victims were recovered from beneath the vehicle. Rescue teams continued their search operation amid fears that more passengers might be trapped under the wreckage. Five rescue vehicles participated in the operation, Rescue 1122 said. Last week, 12 passengers were killed and around two dozen injured when a minibus and a passenger coach collided head-on near Zero Point in Uthal on the Quetta-Karachi Highway in Balochistan. The accident occurred two days after 10 people were killed and 44 others injured when a passenger bus overturned after hitting a road divider in Rajanpur district’s Rojhan tehsil on the Indus Highway on Wednesday.

items.title: L’hubris de Citrini : quand l’IA devient la nouvelle cocaïne des traders
items.description: Mardi 20 octobre, les traders de la firme américaine de recherche en investissement Citrini ont publié un article dans lequel ils annoncent avoir conçu, avec un modèle de recherche interne d’Anthropic, des protéines capables de se lier aux neurotoxines du venin de scorpion Citrini Therapeutics , Citrini Research, 20 octobre 2026.'> 1 . Ces derniers précisent ne rien connaître à la biologie – et aux sciences de manière générale. Le même jour, Anthropic a publié un rapport technique sur cette expérience, menée sur son réseau et ses machines. Les garde-fous de biosécurité du Claude commercialisé avaient en effet bloqué les traders dès leur première requête. En 64 heures, celui-ci a généré plus de 318 000 designs de protéines et en a retenu 180. Avec 31 ajouts ultérieurs, 211 ont été testés en laboratoire et 17 ont rempli les critères de liaison fixés. Le projet, qui a duré trois mois, a coûté à Citrini environ 200 000 dollars, dont 50 000 en puissance de calcul. L’équipe de Citrini revendique avoir fait, en trois mois et à cinq, ce que le développement classique d’un antivenin demande d’ordinaire à des laboratoires spécialisés. Les traders reconnaissent n’avoir mis aucun médicament sur le marché et n’avoir rien publié de scientifiquement significatif, mais estiment toutefois que « la frontière a bougé ». Le plan de bataille des traders de Citrini. Sur la frise du développement d’un médicament, qui court de l’identification de la maladie jusqu’au remboursement par les assurances, l’expérience ne couvre que les deux premières cases. © Citrini Research Comment expliquer ce prodige ? Comme pour Anthropic, qui avait annoncé fin septembre la découverte par Claude d’un système enzymatique inédit à répétitions de type CRISPR, l’objectif principal de Citrini semble être de faire de la publicité. À la fin de l’article, en accès ouvert, ils présentent un autre article, payant, où ils expliquent tout ce que cette « expérience » leur a appris et prodiguent les conseils en investissement que cela leur inspire. La phrase la plus révélatrice de cette expérience est celle où les traders se félicitent que « leur invention digitale va désormais créer du travail pour des scientifiques humains ». On ne peut pas exclure que quelque chose émerge de ces travaux, puisque certaines découvertes majeures ont été faites de façon iconoclaste. Il est cependant très probable que les « scientifiques » pour lesquels ces traders ont « créé du travail » eussent fait un bien meilleur usage des 200 000 dollars que Citrini a engagés dans cette « expérience ». Et étant donné l’état du financement de la recherche, si Citrini y met le prix, il est probable que des chercheurs compétents finissent par travailler sur ses résultats. L’IA aspire déjà une part démesurée du capital disponible, au détriment d’autres projets potentiellement aussi prometteurs. Ce type « d’expériences » fait peser le même risque sur l’allocation des ressources scientifiques. Pendant la pandémie de Covid-19, la controverse sur l’hydroxychloroquine a ainsi poussé soignants et chercheurs à multiplier les protocoles d’essais. Il est assez rapidement apparu que la molécule était probablement efficace in vitro mais inefficace in vivo. La pression populaire a pourtant conduit à continuer à la tester, au détriment d’autres pistes de traitement. Que se passerait-il si demain ce n’étaient plus des traders mais Barron Trump, le fils du président américain, qui annonce la découverte « d’une nouvelle molécule révolutionnaire » grâce à l’IA ? Trump pourrait alors contraindre des chercheurs financés par le gouvernement fédéral à consacrer leur temps et leurs ressources à « investiguer » cette molécule – au détriment d’autres travaux bien plus pertinents. L’article L’hubris de Citrini : quand l’IA devient la nouvelle cocaïne des traders est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: GTEC, TUTAG reach truce to save academic calendar in technical universities
items.description: Teaching and learning across the nation’s technical universities are set to resume shortly following a breakthrough agreement reached between the Technical University Teachers’ Association of Ghana (TUTAG) and government authorities. The industrial dispute, which had threatened to derail the tertiary academic calendar, reached a decisive turning point on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, during high-level conciliation talks involving TUTAG, the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC), and the Vice-Chancellors of Technical Universities of Ghana (VCTU-G). A joint communiqué released at the conclusion of the deliberations indicated that TUTAG has committed to consulting its general membership with a view to immediately suspending its ongoing strike, paving the way for continued negotiations in good faith. The industrial action had been triggered by three primary grievances: delayed remuneration for post-retirement contract staff, a controversial policy directive making a doctorate degree a mandatory requirement for promoting Assistant Lecturers to Lecturers, and the proper designation of academic librarians as full academic staff. Concessions and resolutions On the contentious issue of post-retirement contract salaries, the stakeholders noted that final administrative approval rests with the Ministry of Finance. To resolve the impasse, GTEC pledged to arrange a direct consultative meeting involving the Minister for Finance, university vice-chancellors, and union leadership no later than November 14, 2026. In a significant concession regarding career progression, GTEC agreed to grant a waiver on the PhD promotion requirement for Assistant Lecturers and Assistant Research Fellows who had satisfied their respective institutions’ promotion benchmarks prior to July 31, 2025. Addressing the status of academic librarians, GTEC affirmed that it raises no objection in principle to TUTAG’s demands. It was agreed that the National President of the University Librarians Association will draft and present a comprehensive technical paper to guide final implementation. Reaffirming their mutual commitment to maintaining industrial stability, all parties underscored the necessity of sustained dialogue to prevent future disruptions to higher education in the country.

items.title: ‘We tend to be open-minded and liberal, but that’s not how we’ve lived so far’ – Kufuor
items.description: Former President John Agyekum Kufuor has called for a Ghana that gives individual enterprise room to thrive while ensuring its wealth delivers quality education, healthcare and protection against poverty. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, he said the country’s openness must translate into governance that empowers people to create wealth. “We tend to be open-minded and liberal, but that’s not how we’ve lived so far,” he said. Kufuor was responding to a question about his vision for Ghana over the next 50 years and the future he hopes young people will inherit. He placed good leadership and inclusive governance at the centre of that vision. He argued that Ghana has both the natural resources and human talent to build a prosperous society. But achieving that future would require leaders to recognise individual entrepreneurs’ ability to turn their talents and resources into wealth. “We shouldn’t stifle initiative with excessive taxation,” he stated. He called for an environment where people can build legitimate fortunes, pay reasonable taxes and retain the rewards of their work. In his view, the state should provide the framework that empowers them. “If we do that, allow the private sector to mature, to attract investments, both from within and from outside, the people are happy when they come here.” His vision also puts social protection alongside private enterprise. He said leadership must generate wealth to fund interventions that improve lives. Education was a central priority. “We must ensure that all the children of this land are given some of the finest education you can get anywhere.” He also called for good healthcare and a safety net to protect people with disabilities and those without jobs from abject poverty. Kufuor pointed to Ghana’s mineral resources, including gold, lithium, bauxite and manganese, as evidence of its potential. He also highlighted the character and abilities of its people. He described Ghanaians as people who interact, intermarry and pull together despite their differences. He said they learn well and distinguish themselves abroad. For Kufuor, the task is to turn those advantages into shared prosperity. That means inclusive leadership, space for enterprise and public support that gives every Ghanaian a chance to live well.

items.title: Three arrested over murder of 34-year-old mobile money vendor at Kasoa
items.description: The Central East Regional Police Command has arrested three suspects in connection with the alleged murder of a 34-year-old mobile money vendor, Christian Amponsah, at a guest house around Kasoa Second in the Central Region. The suspects are Felicia Osei Appiah, 59, Clement Opoku Yeboah, 24, and a juvenile female whose identity has not been disclosed. According to a statement signed by the Head of Public Affairs for the Central East Region, DSP Victor Kofi Dosoo. dated October 28, 2026, the arrests were made on Tuesday, October 27, following a report by the manager of the guest house where the deceased and the juvenile had reportedly booked a room for two hours. The manager became concerned when the two failed to leave after the booking period had elapsed. He subsequently went to check on them and allegedly found Mr Amponsah lying motionless in a pool of blood. Police officers who visited the scene found the deceased lying in a prone position, covered with bedsheets, curtains and pillows, the statement said. His body was later conveyed to the Police Hospital mortuary in Accra for preservation, identification and autopsy. The autopsy is expected to assist investigators in establishing the cause of death as investigations continue. The three suspects are in police custody and are assisting with investigations. The police said efforts were underway to complete investigations and put the suspects before court. The command also thanked members of the public and other stakeholders whose information it said had helped the police apprehend the suspects.

items.title: Reconsider 20% excise tax removal on locally produced fruit juices – VAST Ghana to Finance Ministry
items.description: Vision for Accelerated Sustainable Development, Ghana (VAST Ghana) has urged the Finance Ministry to reconsider removing the 20 per cent excise tax on locally produced fruit juices under the Excise Tax Act 2026. It cautioned that the exemption could undermine Ghana’s public health objectives and weaken fiscal policy’s effectiveness in preventing non-communicable diseases (NCDs). A statement copied to the Ghana News Agency by Ms Jennifer Maame Ama Owusu, Communications Manager, VAST Ghana, also urged the Ministry of Health to urgently address the 20 per cent excise tax cut. It noted that the 20 per cent removal could affect the sustainability of the President’s globally acclaimed Ghana Medical Trust Fund, aimed at improving access to treatment and care, and the Free Primary Health Care Policy, which prioritises disease prevention and early intervention. The statement said the decision warranted careful reconsideration from a public health perspective, stating that, “Supporting local businesses is a legitimate economic objective, but such support should not inadvertently encourage the consumption of products that contribute to excessive sugar intake and increase the risk of diet-related diseases.” VAST Ghana also expressed concern about the clarity and robustness of the definition of fruit juice that the Ministry of Finance intends to apply in implementing the exemption. “Ghanaians deserve to know the criteria that will determine which products qualify, particularly given the potential implications for industry profits, public health and domestic revenue mobilisation,” it pointed out. The statement said fruit juices were not automatically healthy alternatives to other sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs), stressing that depending on their composition and processing, they may contain substantial amounts of free sugars, including sugars concentrated during production. It noted that excessive consumption of these beverages could contribute to weight gain, overweight, obesity, type ‘2’ diabetes, and other diet-related NCDs, and that exempting locally produced fruit juices solely on the basis of their origin, without adequately considering their sugar content, risks creating a policy inconsistency in Ghana’s public health tax framework. The statement said Ghana had demonstrated regional and global leadership in addressing NCDs, and that sustaining it required continued investment in well-designed preventive health policies that deliver substantial health, social, and economic benefits. “In this regard, any changes to fiscal policies must also safeguard public health, including by ensuring that the overall tax burden on products that contribute to NCDs remains sufficient to discourage harmful consumption,” it stated. It added that, “Excise taxation is an important public health instrument that can reduce the consumption of harmful products while generating domestic revenue to support national development priorities. “This approach aligns with the World Health Organization’s ‘3 by 35’ initiative, which calls on countries to increase the real prices of tobacco, alcohol, and sugary drinks through effective tax measures by 2035.” The statement said Ghana has made incredible progress in addressing the growing burden of NCDs; however, a fiscal policy intended to support domestic production should complement the government’s ongoing efforts, rather than conflict with national efforts to improve nutrition and prevent NCDs. VAST Ghana therefore urged the Ministry of Finance to adopt a more evidence-based approach that applies excise taxes to beverages based on their free sugar content, regardless of whether they are locally produced or imported. “Such an approach would align taxation more closely with the health risks associated with excessive sugar consumption, promote a level playing field among manufacturers, and create incentives to produce healthier beverages,” it stated. It said a carefully designed sugar-content-based tax could also encourage manufacturers to reduce sugar levels in their products while supporting Ghana’s broader public health and revenue mobilisation objectives. “We, therefore, call on the Ministry of Finance to reconsider the public health implications of the 20 per cent excise tax exemption for locally produced fruit juices in future tax reforms and to work with the Ministry of Health, the Food and Drugs Authority and other relevant stakeholders towards a sugar-content-based approach to taxing beverages. “Ghana must not allow an industrial incentive to weaken the effectiveness of its public health protections,” VAST Ghana urged.

items.title: Bawumia calls for scrapping of proposed pre-shipment vehicle inspection
items.description: New Patriotic Party (NPP) 2028 flagbearer Dr Mahamudu Bawumia has called for the abolition of a proposed pre-shipment inspection requirement for imported vehicles following a meeting with the leadership of the Vehicles and Assets Dealers Union of Ghana (VADUG). The engagement focused on challenges facing vehicle dealers, including high import duties, delays in clearing vehicles at ports, access to credit, and competition from foreign retailers. In a Facebook post, Dr Bawumia said the meeting was part of his stakeholder consultations to understand the industry’s concerns and explore possible policy interventions. He said both sides agreed that the intended introduction of pre-shipment inspection of cars should be abolished. The discussions also covered access to financing from the Ghana Export-Import Bank (EXIM Bank), with dealers seeking improved credit opportunities to support their businesses. Dr Bawumia further highlighted concerns about the enforcement of laws designed to protect Ghanaian retailers from what the union considers unfair competition from foreign retailers. He described the engagement as fruitful and said the respective teams would continue discussions to develop specific policies to address the issues raised. He thanked VADUG’s leadership for making time for the consultation.

TUTAG to suspend strike after talks with GTEC, technical university vice-chancellors
items.description: The Technical University Teachers’ Association of Ghana (TUTAG) is set to suspend its strike after talks with the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) and the Vice-Chancellors of Technical Universities of Ghana (VCTU-G) to resolve the concerns that triggered the industrial action. The parties reached the decision at a meeting on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, where they agreed on measures to address the outstanding issues and restore industrial harmony. In a joint communiqué issued after the meeting, the parties said TUTAG would consult its general membership and immediately suspend the strike while engagements continue towards resolving the concerns. The industrial action centres on the non-payment of staff on post-retirement contracts, a directive requiring a PhD to promote Assistant Lecturers to Lecturers, and the classification of academic librarians as academic staff. On the post-retirement contracts, the parties acknowledged that the matter falls under the Minister for Finance’s remit. GTEC has agreed to facilitate a meeting involving the Minister, vice-chancellors and other stakeholders by November 14, 2026, to work towards a resolution. GTEC has also agreed to exempt affected staff who held the rank of Assistant Lecturer or Assistant Research Fellow and met their universities’ promotion criteria before July 31, 2025, from the PhD requirement for progression to Lecturer. Regarding the classification of academic librarians, GTEC indicated it did not oppose TUTAG’s position in principle. The parties agreed that the National President of the University Librarians Association would submit a technical paper for consideration and implementation. The parties reaffirmed their commitment to continued dialogue and collaboration to maintain industrial harmony and ensure the uninterrupted delivery of teaching and learning in technical universities.

items.title: Inquiry holds school owner responsible for roof collapse
items.description: PESHAWAR: An inquiry into the recent deadly collapse of a school roof here has held the owner responsible for using substandard construction material. It also pointed out negligence on the part of the relevant departments. The inquiry report was presented to Governor Faisal Karim Kundi during a meeting chaired by him here, according to an official statement issued by his office. The meeting was attended by adviser to the governor Dr Amir Abdullah, chief secretary Dr Fakhar Alam Irfan, education secretary Inayatullah Waseem and members of the inquiry committee. At least 30 children and a schoolteacher were killed and dozens of others injured when the roof of a multi-storey private school collapsed in the Dir Colony area. Rescue officials said that the ceiling of a classroom collapsed onto students after the roof of the floor above gave way, causing the two storeys to crumble. The governor later ordered an inquiry into the incident. On Wednesday, the inquiry committee held the school owner responsible for using substandard construction material. The meeting, chaired by the governor, was also briefed about negligence by the relevant departments. Mr Kundi received a detailed briefing on the causes of the incident, statements of the relevant officials, the responsibilities of various departments, the inquiry committee’s findings and its recommendations. The governor directed authorities to examine the legal aspects of the report in consultation with the law department. He said that strict action should be taken against those responsible for the school collapse. Published in Dawn, October 29th, 2026

items.title: Prévisions de la Banque mondiale pour 2027 : bonne et mauvaise nouvelle pour l’Algérie
items.description: La Banque mondiale prévoit une forte hausse des prix de l'énergie et des matières premières cette année ainsi qu'une augmentation des prix des produits alimentaires en 2027. Des prévisions qui constituent pour l’Algérie à la fois une bonne et une mauvaise nouvelle. Par une mécanique simple, les dividendes supplémentaires à engranger des ventes de pétrole et de gaz pourraient être phagocytés par une facture des importations appelée à être plus lourde. El Niño et la guerre en Iran portent les prix vers le haut Les prix sont portés par un épisode exceptionnel à venir du phénomène El Niño et évidemment le conflit du Moyen-Orient. Selon des prévisions de la Banque mondiale révélées ce mercredi 28 octobre dans un communiqué, les prix de l’énergie et des engrais devraient bondir cette année de 32 % et de 14 % respectivement. Quant aux prix des produits alimentaires, ils devraient augmenter en 2027 de 18 % par rapport à leur niveau de 2025. La situation au Moyen-Orient a fait flamber les prix du pétrole et des produits énergétiques. La moyenne des prix du baril est passée de 69 dollars en 2025 à 91 dollars en 2026. Prix de l’énergie et des denrées alimentaires en 2027 : les deux scénarios de la Banque mondiale Pour 2027, la Banque mondiale prévoit deux scénarios antagoniques concernant les prix du pétrole. Si la guerre en Iran ne reprend pas après les élections américaines du 3 novembre, le prix moyen du baril sera de 79 dollars en 2027. Dans le cas contraire, la moyenne s’élèverait à 105 dollars le baril. Ce qui, calcule encore l’institution, ferait augmenter les prix des denrées alimentaires de 12 % supplémentaires par rapport au scénario médian. La hausse des prix du pétrole devrait tirer la demande vers le bas, de 2,5 %, compensant en partie le recul des livraisons estimé à 5,2 %. Ce qui inquiète, c’est le risque pour la sécurité alimentaire mondiale induit par la hausse des prix des produits alimentaires. « La priorité doit être donnée à la protection des populations les plus pauvres et au soutien des pays à faibles revenus, qui doivent déjà faire face à une dette qui pèse lourd », a indiqué Ayhan Kose, chef-économiste adjoint de la Banque mondiale, cité dans le communiqué. Vers le renflouement des caisses de l’Algéri e Pour l'Algérie, l'aspect positif de ces bouleversements, c'est la perspective d’une hausse encore plus conséquente de ses recettes, qui ont déjà fortement rebondi cette année. Dans les neuf premiers mois de 2026, l'Algérie a engrangé 37,5 milliards de dollars de la vente de pétrole et de gaz, a révélé le ministre des Hydrocarbures Mohamed Arkab le 17 octobre. Le ministre a fait état d’une hausse du prix moyen du pétrole brut algérien de 37 % par rapport à la même période de 2025, pour s’établir à environ 97 dollars le baril. Le prix moyen du gaz algérien a aussi augmenté à 11,3 dollars par million d’unités thermiques britanniques (BTU). La hausse des recettes de l’Algérie devrait être encore plus conséquente avec l'augmentation annoncée des prix des engrais, l’un des principaux composants des exportations algériennes hors hydrocarbures. Le renflouement des caisses cette année et très probablement en 2027 est une aubaine pour poursuivre avec une certaine aisance le financement des grands projets d’infrastructures et de la politique sociale de l’État. Gare à l’importation de l’inflation ! Le revers de la médaille, c'est la perspective de la poursuite de la hausse des produits alimentaires, qui constituent une partie importante de la facture des importations algériennes . C'est le cas notamment des céréales, de la poudre de lait, des graines oléagineuses et d'autres produits. En attendant l’entrée en production de plusieurs projets structurants, l’Algérie continue à dépenser chaque année de fortes sommes pour importer ces produits. Si les prévisions de la Banque mondiale se réalisent concernant les denrées alimentaires, l’impact sera double pour l’Algérie. En plus de tirer vers le haut la facture des importations avec un effet mécanique sur la balance des paiements et les réserves de change, il faudra s’attendre aussi à une répercussion sur les niveaux des prix en interne des produits non subventionnés. Ce qui tomberait mal alors que les autorités font tout pour atténuer l’inflation. Comme l’a expliqué le président de la République Abdelmadjid Tebboune devant les opérateurs économiques le 14 octobre, la hausse des prix enregistrée en Algérie est une « inflation importée ». L’article Prévisions de la Banque mondiale pour 2027 : bonne et mauvaise nouvelle pour l’Algérie est apparu en premier sur TSA .
