items.title: Nana Ekuwa Amissah V installed as Anomabo Far Konkohemaa
items.description: Nana Ekuwa Amissah V has been installed as the new Far Konkohemaa (Queen of fishmongers) of Anomabo in the Mfantseman Municipality of the Central Region. Her installation marks a significant transition in the leadership of women in the Anomabo fishing community, coming shortly after the final funeral rites and burial of the late Konkohemaa. As Konkohemaa, Nana Ekuwa Amissah V will be responsible for overseeing the welfare of women in the fishing community, championing their interests and ensuring that their concerns and needs are addressed. The position is particularly important in Anomabo, where women play a crucial role in the fishing value chain through fish processing, preservation, distribution and marketing. The new Konkohemaa is expected to provide leadership and serve as a bridge between the women and traditional authorities, advocating improved livelihoods, access to economic opportunities and better working conditions. She will also be expected to promote unity among the women, help resolve disputes and mobilise support for initiatives aimed at improving their socioeconomic wellbeing. Her installation comes at a time when women in fishing communities continue to face challenges, including fluctuating fish catches, inadequate storage facilities, limited access to credit and rising operational costs. The new Konkohemaa’s leadership is therefore expected to strengthen collaboration among fish processors, traders and other stakeholders to address challenges confronting women in the local fishing industry. The transition follows the passing of Nana Adwoa Amissah IV, whose burial over the weekend paved the way for the installation of her successor in accordance with the community’s traditional leadership arrangements. Beyond preserving the customs and traditions associated with the position, Nana Ekuwa Amissah V is expected to build on the legacy of her predecessor by promoting the economic empowerment and social welfare of women in the fishing community. Her assumption of office represents a new chapter in the leadership of the women, with renewed expectations for unity, advocacy and development. In an interview with the Ghana News Agency after her installation, she promised to promote peace and unity among women within her jurisdiction, ensuring that they were treated fairly and equally.

items.title: Bar Gros, la taberna de barrio que arrasa en el centro de Barcelona:“Por 35 euros sales con el estómago lleno”
items.description: “Abrimos las puertas de nuestro primer restaurante con un cocinero novato. Yo atendía las mesas y servíamos pescado y arroz. O ese era el plan. Empezó a entrar mucha gente y yo quise asegurarme de que la cocina estaba controlada. Así que le dije al cocinero: ‘dos mesas de ocho han pedido arroz . ¿Hay algún problema?’. Y el tipo me contestó: ‘no, no, tira’. Al cabo de unos minutos volví a preguntar: ‘hay otra mesa de seis y también quieren arroz. ¿Algún problema?’. ‘No, no, tira’, insistió. Media hora después y al ver que no salía nada de la cocina, fui a mirar: el delantal estaba allí bien colocado, pero del cocinero no había ni rastro. Se había largado”. Lo cuenta riendo Jordi Millán (1981, Barcelona) quien junto a su mujer Sara Martín (1983, Barcelona) lleva desde 2014 poniendo patas arriba la capital catalana. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Marrakech: le Jardin Majorelle inaugure son deuxième pavillon temporaire
items.description: Le Jardin Majorelle a inauguré, mercredi, à Marrakech, son deuxième pavillon temporaire baptisé « Nouala, le refuge mobile » et conçu par l'architecte marocaine Salsabil El Ouazzani, lauréate du prix Fondation Jardin Majorelle 2026. Diplômée de l'Université Mohammed VI Polytechnique, Salsabil El Ouazzani a remporté, le 15 mai 2026 à Marrakech, la 2e édition de ce concours national dédié à la relève de l'architecture marocaine, en s'imposant face à 33 autres candidatures. Quelques mois après avoir remporté cette distinction, l'architecte a vu ainsi son projet prendre forme au cœur de la Cité Ocre, à travers une structure qui revisite la nouala, une hutte traditionnelle des campagnes marocaines, construite à partir de roseaux et de chaume, avec les ressources disponibles dans son environnement. En associant cette référence à l'idée d'un refuge en mouvement, Salsabil El Ouazzani a puisé dans la mémoire vernaculaire collective pour proposer une interprétation contemporaine de cet abri traditionnel. Installé dans le jardin de la Villa Oasis, ce pavillon, qui accueille l'exposition « Les oiseaux du Jardin Majorelle », se caractérise par une structure légère et démontable, réalisée à partir de matériaux simples et naturels, dont l'assemblage privilégie la sobriété et la réversibilité. Conçu comme un espace de transition et de contemplation, ce pavillon invite les visiteurs à cheminer au cœur de la végétation, tout en leur offrant une expérience intime en dialogue avec le paysage du Jardin Majorelle. Le jury a été sensible à la pertinence des matériaux retenus, à la délicatesse avec laquelle la structure s'intègre à la végétation, à la précision du dessin et au réalisme de sa mise en œuvre, dans le cadre d'une compétition particulièrement serrée. Le président de la Fondation Jardin Majorelle, Madison Cox était entouré d'un jury composé de Karl Fournier, cofondateur de Studio KO, de l'architecte et anthropologue Salima Naji et d'Alexis Sornin, directeur du musée Pierre Bergé des arts berbères et du musée Yves Saint Laurent Marrakech. À cette occasion, Cox a souligné que ce pavillon temporaire s'inscrit dans une démarche visant à faire du Jardin Majorelle un espace d'expérimentation pour les talents émergents de l'architecture marocaine, en leur offrant une vitrine exceptionnelle au sein de l'un des sites culturels les plus visités du Royaume. Il a, également, mis en avant le caractère renouvelable de cette initiative, chaque nouvelle version du pavillon étant confiée, tous les deux ans, au lauréat du prix Fondation Jardin Majorelle. De son côté, l'architecte Salsabil El Ouazzani a indiqué que son projet s'inspire de l'abri rural traditionnel marocain, léger, adaptable et construit à partir des ressources du lieu, afin d'en proposer une version contemporaine en harmonie avec la végétation du jardin de la Villa Oasis. Ainsi, le dialogue entre le pavillon et son contenu se prolonge à travers l'exposition « Les oiseaux du Jardin Majorelle », présentée depuis avril 2026 et consacrée aux espèces d'oiseaux qui fréquentent le site au fil de l'année. Plus d'une trentaine d'espèces, insectivores, granivores ou omnivores, trouvent refuge dans le jardin. Raphaël Musseau, Rhimou El Hamoumi et Mohamed Radi, spécialistes d'ornithologie et d'écologie, ont apporté leur contribution scientifique à cette exposition. Le parcours met en lumière les conditions qui favorisent la présence de ces oiseaux, notamment l'étagement de la végétation, des plantes herbacées jusqu'aux grands arbres, ainsi que les recoins propices à la nidification et les points d'eau où les oiseaux viennent boire et se baigner. À partir de ce jeudi 29 octobre, les visiteurs pourront découvrir la nouala imaginée par Salsabil El Ouazzani, avant de poursuivre leur parcours à la découverte des oiseaux qui peuplent les allées du jardin. items.title: 3ᵉ Sommet Russie-Afrique à Moscou : La pensée de Thomas Sankara convoquée par Vladimir Poutine pour prôner la souveraineté
items.description: À l'ouverture du troisième Forum économique et humanitaire Russie–Afrique, ce mercredi 28 octobre 2026 au Centre Gostiny Dvor de Moscou, le débat sur le développement souverain du continent a pris une résonance historique particulière. En présence du Premier ministre burkinabè Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo représentant le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré et d'une vingtaine de chefs d'État, le Président russe Vladimir Poutine a expressément cité la pensée du Capitaine Thomas Sankara sur la dette et le néocolonialisme pour plaider en faveur d'un monde multipolaire. Entre appels de l'Union africaine à la transformation locale des matières premières et volonté de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES) de sceller des alliances stratégiques, ce rendez-vous moscovite entend poser les jalons d'un partenariat économique débarrassé des schémas de dépendance. Trente-neuf ans après le célèbre discours de Addis-Abeba, la voix du Capitaine Thomas Sankara s'est de nouveau invitée dans les hautes sphères de la diplomatie internationale. Prenant la parole lors de l'ouverture du troisième Forum économique et humanitaire Russie–Afrique, le Président russe Vladimir Poutine a convoqué la mémoire du héros de la révolution burkinabè pour dénoncer le piège de la dette : « La dette, c’est encore le néocolonialisme, où les colonialistes se sont transformés en assistants techniques » . Soulignant que ces mots prononcés en 1987 restent d'une brûlante actualité, le chef de l'État russe a fustigé les mécanismes financiers internationaux qui brident la souveraineté économique des nations africaines. Défendant l'émergence d'un ordre mondial multipolaire, il a réclamé une représentativité accrue pour le continent africain au sein des institutions financières globales telles que le FMI et la Banque mondiale. Au sein du parterre de dirigeants réunis à Moscou, le Premier ministre burkinabè, le Camarade Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, a porté le message du Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, aux côtés de personnalités clés comme le Président de la Transition du Mali, le Général d'Armée Assimi Goïta. Pour les pays membres de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES), cette présence symbolise une volonté affirmée de diversifier leurs alliances sécuritaires et économiques. Au Burkina Faso, la Révolution progressiste populaire (RPP) conduite par le Capitaine Traoré s'inscrit en droite ligne de cet héritage sankariste, plaçant la mobilisation populaire, la maîtrise des ressources et la production locale au centre de la stratégie de refondation nationale. Également présent à la tribune, le Président du Burundi et Président en exercice de l'Union africaine, Évariste Ndayishimiye, a exhorté les partenaires à concrétiser les engagements bilatéraux par des résultats tangibles pour les populations. Le représentant de l'organisation continentale a plaidé pour une rupture nette avec le modèle traditionnel d'exportation de ressources brutes, appelant à privilégier l'industrialisation, la transformation sur place, les transferts de technologies et la création d’emplois pour la jeunesse. Il a notamment insisté sur la modernisation des réseaux logistiques, le développement de systèmes de paiement indépendants et la stimulation des investissements créateurs de valeur ajoutée dans les domaines de l'énergie et de l'agro-industrie. Au-delà des prises de parole politiques, les travaux du sommet se concentrent sur des axes d'intervention très concrets : énergie, santé, éducation, agriculture et technologies numériques. À l'issue des sessions plénières, Vladimir Poutine a convié les délégations africaines à visiter une exposition dédiée aux innovations industrielles et financières russes de dernière génération. Cette immersion technique ouvre la voie à de futurs partenariats structurants, axés sur le transfert de savoir-faire et le renforcement des capacités productives autonomes des États africains. L’article 3ᵉ Sommet Russie-Afrique à Moscou : La pensée de Thomas Sankara convoquée par Vladimir Poutine pour prôner la souveraineté est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Yemen: Houthis Depriving Taizz Civilians of Food, Medicine
items.description: Click to expand Image The Hayjat al-Abd road, which connects Aden to Taizz city, Yemen, September 26, 2026. © 2026 Photo by AFP via Getty Images (Beirut) – A long-running humanitarian crisis in Taizz, Yemen’s third-largest city, has drastically worsened since October 2026, when the Houthi armed group forces fully encircled the city and blocked and attacked the remaining major supply route, Human Rights Watch said today. Since then, there have been severe shortages of fuel, food, water, medicine, cooking gas, and access by humanitarian agencies. Houthi forces have surrounded Taizz since 2015, early in the conflict with the Yemeni government. While government-backed forces control the city center, Houthi forces have blocked access to all major roads connecting Taizz to the rest of the country, with the road connecting Taizz with Aden the most important. While international law does not prohibit sieges of military forces, the Houthis’ siege has for 12 years severely restricted civilian movement and impeded essential goods to the city’s residents. “Renewed efforts by the Houthis to cut off food, water, and medicine to Taizz show their utter disregard for civilian lives,” said Niku Jafarnia, Yemen and Bahrain researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Throughout the 12-year-long siege of Taizz, the Houthis have bombed, starved, and denied humanitarian aid to a million residents of the city with scant adherence to international law.” The Houthis should immediately open vital roads for essential goods and aid to civilians in Taizz. All warring parties need to facilitate aid and the safe movement of civilians. Human Rights Watch spoke to fifteen people in October, including five city residents, four doctors and six civil society workers. A Houthi spokesperson told Human Rights Watch on October 21 that Yemeni government forces, not Houthi forces, were blocking roads into the city. But residents, civil society workers, and United Nations officials placed responsibility for the shortages on the Houthis. One resident told Human Rights Watch early in the escalation in fighting that vegetables were already “in very short supply” and that their prices had doubled. Another said on October 15 that he had been searching for wheat and flour for three days without finding any. On October 14, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) said that they had not been able to access the “more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance,” which was “especially alarming” since most of Taizz’s districts are considered to have emergency levels of hunger. The WFP also said that “wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted” in the city and that “remaining food supplies in local markets may last only a short time if access constraints continue.” On October 23, Jens Laerke, spokesperson for the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) stated that it had been “20 days and counting since Taiz has been cut off.” The humanitarian crisis in Taizz appears to have been primarily caused by the Houthis cutting off the city from the rest of Yemen, which affects not only deliveries of food, but also water, fuel, and medicine, Human Rights Watch said. “The crisis in Taizz isn’t in the food itself, it’s in the fuel,” said the leader of a local civil society group. “Transporting food depends on fuel… and truck drivers’ costs have doubled.” Residents described the difficulty in obtaining food and cooking gas since the siege tightened. One resident, who runs an organization that provides aid, said that the price of cooking gas had increased by about 400 percent. Others said that bottles of cooking gas had become hard to find. Shortages of fuel have contributed to shortages of water. Akhil Iyer, the country representative in Yemen for the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said that “diesel shortages threaten to bring water pumps to a halt, while the cost of trucked water has tripled since this latest escalation.” Laurent Bukera, the UN humanitarian coordinator for Yemen, said in an October 20 statement that water production had been halved in Taizz city and that alternatives were “running out.” The Houthis have restricted access to water for Taizz residents throughout the long siege, which Human Rights Watch previously found violated residents’ right to water. The Houthis have also been blocking water trucks: an organization tracking the siege said that water tank operators told them that they had been stopped at Houthi checkpoints when trying to bring water into the city. The Houthi siege has severely affected health care for civilians in Taizz, Human Rights Watch said. Doctors and other health workers reported that road closures and fuel shortages prevented many civilians needing health care—especially those with cancer, kidney disease, hypertension, and other chronic diseases living outside the city center—from reaching hospitals and clinics. One doctor said that patients living in government-controlled areas where there were no road closures still struggled to reach healthcare facilities in Taizz “because transportation is difficult and fuel, including gasoline, is unavailable or unaffordable.” Health workers described shortages of medicine and other healthcare items. A doctor in Taizz said that she had seen many patients, including women and children, coming in with conflict-related injuries, but that there was a shortage of anesthesia for surgeries. Others said that stocks of essential medicines and other medical supplies were running dangerously low. A health worker said that a shortage of oxygen posed “an additional threat to essential health services, emergency surgeries, intensive care, dialysis, and neonatal care.” One doctor said: “Most health supplies come from Aden to Taizz, but now, due to the siege, road closures, and armed clashes, transporting them has become extremely difficult and more costly than before.” Fuel shortages have also affected healthcare facilities, many of which rely on generators that use diesel. One doctor said that his facility had to “stop working for three days because we run out of diesel. Patients were coming and leaving disappointed, as there is no service or care we can offer them.” Bukera said in his October 20 statement that Taizz’s “health system is close to collapse,” and that shortages “threaten hospital energy supply and medical oxygen availability, putting hundreds of patients’ lives at risk.” International humanitarian law applicable to the armed conflict in Yemen does not prohibit siege warfare so long as the purpose is to achieve a military objective and not to starve or cause disproportionate harm to the civilian population. Starvation can include the intentional deprivation of medicine and other necessities, in addition to food and water. All warring parties, including a besieging army, have an obligation to facilitate access of humanitarian aid to civilians and not arbitrarily delay it. Parties must also ensure the freedom of movement of humanitarian workers, which can only be restricted temporarily for reasons of imperative military necessity. Customary international humanitarian law prohibits as a war crime the use of starvation of civilians as a method of warfare by depriving them of objects indispensable to their survival, including by impeding relief supplies. Criminal intent can be inferred from the totality of the circumstances of the military campaign and does not require that people in fact starved. “The Houthis cannot use the siege of Taizz to justify the humanitarian catastrophe they are causing civilians,” Jafarnia said. “They should immediately facilitate the entry of food, fuel, medicine, water, and aid to avert further suffering.”

items.title: 23ᵉ session ordinaire du CNLS-IST : 138,12 milliards FCFA mobilisés pour éliminer le Sida au Burkina Faso d’ici à 2030
items.description: Présidée ce mercredi 28 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou par le Ministre Directeur de cabinet du Président du Faso, le Capitaine Martha Céleste Anderson Medah représentant le Chef de l’État, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré , la 23ᵉ session ordinaire du Conseil national de Lutte contre le Sida et les Infections sexuellement transmissibles (CNLS-IST) a scellé un tournant stratégique majeur. À cette occasion, les membres du conseil ont adopté le nouveau Plan stratégique national (PSN-SIDA 2026-2030), doté d'un budget de 138,12 milliards de FCFA. Ce nouveau cadre d'action vise à intensifier la riposte sanitaire afin d'éliminer définitivement le Sida en tant que problème de santé publique au Burkina Faso d'ici à 2030. La capitale burkinabè a accueilli ce mercredi la 23ᵉ session ordinaire du Conseil national de Lutte contre le Sida et les Infections sexuellement transmissibles (CNLS-IST). Les travaux de cette haute instance de concertation ont été présidés par le Ministre Directeur de cabinet du Président du Faso, le Camarade Capitaine Martha Céleste Anderson Medah, représentant le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, Chef de l’État et président du CNLS-IST. Cette rencontre d'envergure avait pour mission d'évaluer le chemin parcouru et de fixer la trajectoire de la santé publique nationale pour les cinq prochaines années. Au cours de la session, les participants ont passé en revue la mise en œuvre des recommandations de l'édition précédente et dressé le bilan d'étape du Plan national multisectoriel (PNM) 2025. L'acte central de cette réunion a été l'examen et la validation du Plan stratégique national de lutte contre le VIH, le Sida et les IST (PSN-SIDA) pour la période 2026-2030. Évalué à 138,12 milliards de FCFA , ce nouveau plan stratégique constitue la feuille de route financière et opérationnelle destinée à accélérer la dynamique de riposte pour éradiquer la maladie en tant que problème de santé publique à l'horizon 2030. Prenant la parole au nom du Chef de l'État, le Capitaine Martha Céleste Anderson Medah a salué la mobilisation constante de l'ensemble des acteurs engagés dans la lutte contre le VIH et les IST. Il a souligné la portée charnière de cette rencontre, qui marque la clôture formelle du Cadre stratégique national 2021-2025 et ouvre une nouvelle phase décisive avec l'entrée en vigueur du PSN-SIDA 2026-2030. L’article 23ᵉ session ordinaire du CNLS-IST : 138,12 milliards FCFA mobilisés pour éliminer le Sida au Burkina Faso d'ici à 2030 est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Diplomatie : À Moscou, le Premier ministre réaffirme le refus de toute tutelle sur le Burkina Faso
items.description: Le Burkina Faso entend construire des partenariats fondés sur le respect mutuel, l’égalité entre les États et la défense de sa souveraineté. C’est le message porté par le Premier ministre, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, lors d’un entretien exclusif accordé au média russe RT, le 27 octobre 2026, en marge du troisième Sommet Russie–Afrique à Moscou. Interrogé par le journaliste Igor Kurashenko, le Chef du Gouvernement a réaffirmé la volonté du Burkina Faso de rester maître de ses choix politiques, économiques et diplomatiques. Il a dénoncé les rapports de domination, les accords déséquilibrés et les ingérences extérieures, estimant que la rupture avec la politique impérialiste française s’inscrit dans une dynamique d’émancipation nationale. « Nous n’avons rien contre le peuple français », a-t-il déclaré, en distinguant le peuple français des orientations politiques qu’il conteste. Pour le Premier ministre, le peuple burkinabè doit pouvoir décider librement de son avenir et défendre ses propres intérêts. Coopérer sans changer de tutelle Répondant aux critiques qui présentent le rapprochement avec la Russie comme un simple changement de partenaire dominant, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo a rappelé que le Burkina Faso recherchait une nouvelle forme de coopération, et non une nouvelle dépendance. « Nous avons quitté un type de coopération pour un autre type de coopération », a-t-il affirmé, plaidant pour des relations transparentes, équilibrées et mutuellement bénéfiques. À travers sa participation au sommet, le Burkina Faso entend notamment renforcer la formation, favoriser les transferts de technologies et développer ses capacités nationales de production. L’ambition affichée est de produire davantage pour répondre aux besoins alimentaires, transformer les ressources minières sur le territoire national et valoriser les compétences locales. Ces priorités s’inscrivent dans la vision de développement portée par le Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, qui met l’accent sur la souveraineté économique et la mobilisation des ressources nationales. Reconquête du territoire et coopération sécuritaire La situation sécuritaire a également occupé une place importante dans cet entretien. Le Premier ministre a évoqué une amélioration progressive de la situation sur le terrain, en mettant en avant le chiffre de plus de 74 % du territoire consolidé. Selon ses explications, ce taux concerne les zones reconquises, sécurisées durablement et dans lesquelles des populations déplacées ont pu regagner leurs localités. Il a par ailleurs souligné la contribution du partenariat avec la Russie au renforcement des capacités des Forces combattantes, notamment à travers la prise en main des équipements et le développement des compétences opérationnelles. L’AES face aux campagnes de désinformation Au-delà des enjeux diplomatiques et sécuritaires, le Chef du Gouvernement a insisté sur la dimension informationnelle de la lutte pour la souveraineté. Il a dénoncé les campagnes de désinformation visant les pays de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES), composée du Burkina Faso, du Mali et du Niger. Pour les autorités burkinabè, la défense de la souveraineté passe également par la capacité des États sahéliens à faire entendre leurs positions et à nouer des relations internationales respectueuses de leurs choix. À Moscou, le message du Premier ministre est ainsi resté centré sur une orientation : diversifier les partenariats sans renoncer à l’indépendance de décision du Burkina Faso. Pour Ouagadougou, l’enjeu est désormais de faire de cette coopération un levier concret de transformation économique, de renforcement des capacités nationales et de consolidation de la souveraineté. Source : DCRP/Primature L’article Diplomatie : À Moscou, le Premier ministre réaffirme le refus de toute tutelle sur le Burkina Faso est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Moscow’s Afghan outreach
items.description: RUSSIA’S growing engagement with Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers is reshaping the regional diplomatic landscape. For Pakistan, which has historically maintained close links with Afghan political and religious networks, the development presents both a challenge and an opportunity. The question is not whether Moscow will replace Islamabad as Kabul’s principal interlocutor, but whether Russia’s expanding diplomatic, security and economic engagement will give the Taliban greater room to manoeuvre in their dealings with Pakistan. Russia’s approach towards the Taliban has been gradually shaping up. In July 2025, Moscow became the first country to recognise the Taliban government formally. Earlier, it announced the removal of the Taliban from its list of prohibited terrorist organisations in April that year. In May 2026, Russian officials announced plans to establish a “full-fledged partnership” with Kabul, encompassing security, trade, cultural exchanges, and humanitarian cooperation. That same month, a military-technical cooperation arrangement further underscored the deepening relationship. Moscow, therefore, has been moving beyond limited diplomatic engagement towards a more sustained relationship with the Taliban authorities. Multiple factors may be shaping Moscow’s approach toward the Taliban. First, Moscow remains concerned about the spread of militant violence into Central Asia, narcotics trafficking, and the activities of Islamic State-Khorasan (IS-K). The deadly 2024 attack near Moscow reinforced Russian concerns about transnational extremist networks. From the Kremlin’s perspective, dealing with the Taliban is a pragmatic necessity — whatever its reservations about the nature of their government, the Taliban exercise effective control over Afghan­istan’s state institutions and security apparatus. In parallel, Russia seeks to preserve its influence in Eurasia and prevent Afghanistan from becoming a source of instability that could invite renewed intervention by external powers. Economic cooperation, including potential opportunities in energy, transport, agriculture, and infrastructure, adds another dimension to this policy. Moscow’s outreach should, therefore, be understood as an effort to protect its own interests and expand its regional options. Russia’s close ties with Kabul won’t automatically ensure action against anti-Pakistan terrorists. Second, Russia’s recognition of the Taliban has important implications for Pakistan’s diplomatic leverage. For years, Islamabad’s geographical proximity, economic connections, and historical links with the Taliban gave it considerable access to Kabul. Russian recognition gives Kabul an additional source of international legitimacy. Its expanding relations with Moscow also offer the Taliban another channel for diplomatic engagement, security cooperation, and economic opportunity. The more external partners Kabul acqui­res, the less dependent it may feel on Islamabad for diplomatic access and international engagement. This does not mean that Pakistan’s influence will disappear. Geography, cross-border commerce, people-to-people links, and the management of shared security concerns remain important. However, these factors do not automatically translate into political compliance. Pakistan’s leverage will increasingly depend on whether it can demonstrate the mutual benefits of cooperation rather than rely on historical relationships or geographical realities alone. Third, Russia’s approach to the TTP will be the most consequential test. Islamabad’s central secu­­rity concern is that terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory threaten Pakistan’s citizens and security personnel. The Taliban authorities’ generalised statement is that Afghan territory will not be used against other countries, but they are reluctant to specifically say that Afghan territory will not be allowed to be used against Pakistan. Moscow’s priorities, however, do not match Pakistan’s. Russia’s immediate security concerns centre particularly on IS-K and the threat of extremist violence spreading into Central Asia and Russia itself. Although the Taliban also oppose IS-K, this convergence does not necessarily mean Moscow will place Pakistan’s concerns about the TTP at the centre of its Afghan policy. Pakistan should, therefore, avoid assuming that Russia’s close relations with Kabul will automatically produce action against anti-Pakistan terrorists. Russian influence could provide an additional diplomatic channel, but its effectiveness will depend on Moscow’s willingness to address the TTP issue and the Taliban leadership’s readiness to respond. Fourth, Russia’s interest in regional stability gives it a potential role in facilitating dialogue, reducing tensions and encouraging practical cooperation. Pakistan should welcome constructive Russian involvement without outsourcing its Afghan policy to Moscow. The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation could provide a useful multilateral framework. Pakistan, Russia, China, and the Central Asian states share an interest in preventing Afghanistan from becoming a base for transnational terrorism. Coordinated intelligence exchanges, border-security cooperation, counter-narcotics measures, and structured consultations with Kabul could help establish a regional approach. Such cooperation would be more sustainable than expecting any single country to exercise decisive influence over the Taliban. Fifth, Pakistan needs to adapt its Afghan policy to a more competitive diplomatic environment. Islamabad should deepen engagement with Russia while maintaining direct communication with the Taliban leadership. It should also coordinate with China, the Central Asian republics, and other relevant regional actors to develop a common understanding of the threats emanating from Afghanistan. At the bilateral level, Pakistan has to involve the Taliban in a meaningful dialogue and create a workable environment that builds the Taliban regime’s stake in the mutual benefits of the two countries. This could include arrangements to exchange information on terrorist networks, investigate cross-border incidents, prevent attacks, and maintain communication between security officials. Economic cooperation and the facilitation of legitimate trade should accompany these measures, giving both sides practical incentives to reduce tensions. Diplomatically, Russia’s Afghan outreach is thus neither an inevitable strategic setback for Pakistan nor a guarantee of improved regional security. It is a development that reflects the Tali­ban’s efforts to widen their international options and Moscow’s decision to protect its own interests. Whether this produces greater stability or further competition will depend on how regional states use their expanding diplomatic channels. Pakistan will have to carefully observe that Russia’s engagement helps address the region’s shared security concerns. Islamabad’s influence over Kabul will ultimately depend less on who has the closest relationship with the Taliban and more on who can help produce practical results: a secure border, action against militant violence, functioning trade routes and a stable regional environment. The writer is a former special representative of Pakistan for Afghanistan. He served as Pakistan’s ambassador to the UAE and Iran. Published in Dawn, October 29th, 2026

items.title: India: Mass Voter Roll Exclusions Deeply Flawed
items.description: Click to expand Image Protesters demand the scrapping of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the resignation of India’s top election official, in Hyderabad, India, on October 24, 2026. © 2026 Jwala Kotesh/NurPhoto via AP Photo The Indian authorities’ removal of over 130 million names from the country’s electoral rolls was arbitrary and deeply flawed.Indian authorities first stripped millions of citizens of their right to vote and are now beating and jailing them for peacefully protesting these rights violations.The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services. (London) – The Indian authorities’ removal of over 130 million names from the country’s electoral rolls is arbitrary and deeply flawed, Human Rights Watch said today. In October 2026, tens of thousands of people across India began demonstrating against the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR). The process purportedly removed dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters, but has been arbitrary and opaque and has disproportionately excluded women, people living in poverty, religious minorities, especially Muslims, and people from other marginalized communities. In October, the Election Commission submitted an affidavit to the Supreme Court defending its functioning and rejecting all allegations of irregularities. “Indian authorities first stripped millions of citizens of their right to vote and are now beating and jailing them for peacefully protesting these rights violations,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services.” The protesters have demanded that the process should be scrapped and that the country’s top election official should resign. The authorities responded with the heavy deployment of security personnel, who committed widespread abuses against protesters and journalists covering the protests. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government should immediately end the crackdown on peaceful protests, appropriately prosecute those responsible for abuses, restore every citizen’s right to participate in elections, and establish an independent investigation into allegations of politically motivated interference. Since August, Human Rights Watch has interviewed 70 people in Delhi and the states of West Bengal, Maharashtra, and Karnataka, including 40 people whose families were affected by the SIR process, as well as former election commissioners, lawyers, civil society activists, and a current electoral official. Under India’s Constitution, the Election Commission of India is authorized to revise and update voter rolls, provided that it records its reasons in writing. Ashok Lavasa, a former election commissioner, said that while the commission had routinely updated electoral rolls, it had never before effectively scrapped the voter rolls for the entire country and started the process anew. “The onus of maintaining a clean, updated electoral roll was always on the election commission,” Lavasa said. “It was never on the elector, where he or she had to apply, and if they didn’t apply, their constitutional right would be excluded.” The SIR process began in June 2025 in states with upcoming local elections, requiring voters to show documents proving their eligibility to vote. The process placed a special burden on many in India, especially women and those from socially and economically marginalized communities, who find it difficult to obtain government documents. In addition, the commission adopted arbitrary criteria such as “logical discrepancies” to delete voters who possessed the required documents, modified its rules and forms mid-process without transparency, and used an opaque software system that by its own admission was malfunctioning. The media reported in several states that people had submitted applications seeking to have Muslims deleted from voter lists in bulk. India’s election law allows third parties to object to someone’s inclusion in voter rolls, but it is generally meant for reasons such as death or duplicate entry. Opposition parties and civil society activists allege that the commission has manipulated electoral rolls to benefit the ruling BJP. The Election Commission has not defined the term “logical discrepancies” in any written communication, but Human Rights Watch found that people were arbitrarily excluded for mismatched names, spelling errors, having six or more siblings, or even siblings born less than nine months apart, which would flag most twins. A 26-year-old Muslim tailor with three brothers and four sisters in the South 24 Parganas district in West Bengal said his name was flagged under the “logical discrepancy” list because he had more than five siblings. Five of his siblings were flagged, while three made it into the rolls. “Everyone had documents but despite that our names were deleted,” he said, noting that his family has been on the voter rolls for generations. Even though millions of names had been eliminated from the voter rolls, the Supreme Court in May 2026 ruled that the data did not indicate “systemic disenfranchisement.” And while the court also said that the SIR process did not determine citizenship, BJP state governments in West Bengal and Bihar announced that people whose names were deleted from voter rolls would no longer be eligible for certain government social security programs, including food subsidies. Human Rights Watch found that the authorities have used SIR data to deny government services including passport renewals, social security benefits such as a West Bengal cash assistance program for women, scholarships, and residency certificates needed for college admission. India is a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which guarantees every citizen the right to take part in the conduct of public affairs, to vote and be elected at genuine periodic elections, and to have access to public services without discrimination or unreasonable restrictions. The United Nations Human Rights Committee, which provides authoritative guidance on the covenant, has stated in its General Comment No. 25 that state authorities are obligated to take effective measures to facilitate and not impose obstacles to voter registration, and they must require that any conditions imposed for exercising the right to vote must be objective, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory. India’s Special Intensive Revision process has been neither reasonable nor proportionate, has imposed unnecessary procedural burdens on millions of people, and could lead to mass disenfranchisement, in violation of India’s international legal obligations, Human Rights Watch said. “The disproportionate removal of Muslims and other groups of voters from the rolls raises serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections, crucial to holding governments accountable,” Pearson said. “The government should ensure that all those wrongfully removed from voter rolls promptly regain their voting rights and no one loses access to social security and other programs.” An Arbitrary Process India had 960 million registered voters ahead of 2024 general elections. The last intensive revision of voter rolls, between 2002 and 2006, involved enumerators—field workers who collect information about households—conducting door-to-door verification using preliminary lists generated from the then-existing rolls, with strict supervision and monitoring requirements. “It was the inclusive approach and friendly procedure that the Election Commission of India historically followed which enabled the inclusion of more than 98 percent of the eligible adult population in the electoral roll, one of the highest for any functioning electoral democracy,” said Lavasa, the former election commissioner. For the 2025-2026 revision, the Election Commission has instead applied an evolving set of rules across what it describes as three phases of the SIR. In the first phase, in Bihar just months before legislative elections in November 2025, voters had to fill out enumeration forms and provide 1 of 11 documents from an approved list to prove their eligibility. In August 2025, the Supreme Court directed the Election Commission to add a national biometric identity document, the Aadhaar card, to that list. Nearly 4.7 million names were deleted from the state’s voter rolls. In a second phase, in 10 states and 2 union territories, the Election Commission introduced a step called “mapping” in which voters had to trace themselves or a parent to the electoral rolls prepared during the 2002-2006 intensive revision. The poll body also began deleting names from the rolls for what it called “logical discrepancies,” which had no clear definition or legal basis. Voters flagged for a logical discrepancy receive notices and are required to appear for hearings with electoral registration officers mandated to prepare and publish the electoral rolls. “We never knew anything about logical discrepancies during our training,” said a primary school teacher in West Bengal serving as a booth-level officer, who verifies and updates the electoral roll for a specific polling booth. “The process was haphazard and I only received three days of training from election officials before the SIR began,” he said. “And once the exercise began, the rules kept changing.” As the process went on, the rules were often arbitrarily altered. In West Bengal, for instance, the number of voters under suspicion fell from 16.7 million to about 9.5 million within weeks after a public outcry. Muslims, who historically do not vote for the BJP because it promotes Hindu majoritarianism, were disproportionately targeted. In one constituency, Patharpratima in South 24 Parganas, over 92 percent of those deleted were Muslims, though Muslims constitute only 9 percent of the population. Shortly afterward, in the April 2025 election, the BJP won control of the state for the first time, while the Supreme Court effectively said it was acceptable for those excluded not to be able to vote that time so long as they would be added back to the rolls. About 93 percent of the voters in West Bengal whose appeals were decided were eventually restored to the rolls, showing that 9 out of every 10 voters removed from the voter list were wrongfully removed. The Calcutta High Court said, however, that it would take at least 21 years to resolve over 3.4 million appeals to the deletions still pending in the appellate tribunals. In the third and final phase, ongoing in 16 states and 3 union territories, the electoral body modified Form 6 used to enroll new voters, requiring additional information from applicants about whether their parents or grandparents were part of the previous intensive revision. Two election commissioners reportedly objected to these changes, but the electoral body claimed it had Supreme Court permission to add the requirement. The chief justice of India said the court had not approved the change. The Election Commission has also directed states to use Form 6 to reenroll voters who had been deleted from lists, even though these were not new voters but rather those who had voted in previous elections. This required voters to falsely declare that they were applying for the first time, a criminal offense that carries a jail term of up to a year. Misuse of Objection Forms for Bulk Deletions Form 7 allows third parties to object to anyone’s inclusion on the electoral rolls. Media reports show that people in several states filed this form in bulk to systematically object to eligible Muslim voters. When an objection is filed, electoral registration officers may accept an objection if they are satisfied or conduct a hearing by giving notice to the relevant parties. Individual electors were only allowed to file six such forms online, but there was no limit on the number of paper forms they could submit, allowing bulk filing. Opposition leaders and civil society groups accused BJP booth-level agents of misusing the form to file objections in bulk. Until 2023, these agents could file up to 10 forms a day, but they were allowed to file up to 50 forms per day once the SIR was underway in October 2025. In Karnataka, Deputy Chief Minister DK Shivakumar demanded a police inquiry into bulk deletions, and in some districts police cases were filed against BJP workers. In two assembly constituencies in Uttar Pradesh, about 90 percent of the deletion forms were filed against Muslim voters. Five men reportedly linked to the BJP filed 6,500 deletion applications against Muslim voters in Uttarakhand. In May 2026, the Gujarat High Court issued a notice to the state and its election authorities over allegations of targeted deletions. In October, the Election Commission applied stricter limits, allowing each elector to file only 10 forms throughout the claims and objections period. Exclusions Driven by Opaque Software The SIR process uses software to which no one outside the Election Commission has access; the technology has long been opaque and there are reasons to question its reliability. The Election Commission scanned and digitized the paper electoral rolls of 2002 to 2006 and printed the rolls in several Indian language scripts that were transliterated into English by the software, without any publicly established standards to maintain accuracy, the New Delhi-based Internet Freedom Foundation found. This seemingly flawed database provided the baseline for voter eligibility during the first step of the 2025 process, when every voter form was keyed into the system and then traced back to previous rolls. Technologies, including purpose-built or proprietary software designed and deployed for public use, should be subject to public scrutiny, Human Rights Watch said. In December 2025, the office of West Bengal’s chief electoral officer said that the software was malfunctioning because the 2002 data “had not been digitized accurately.” And as Human Rights Watch and others have found, the software has disproportionately flagged names from Adivasi, or indigenous, and Muslim communities for “logical discrepancies,” in part because the spelling of names in such communities is more fluid: for example, Md, Mohammed, Mohd, or Mohammad are variants of the same name; Sk, Shaikh, Sheikh, or Sheik are also equivalents. Md Shamim Akhtar, a former wing commander in the Indian air force, found his name was deleted from electoral rolls in West Bengal in March 2026. He said that he did not receive any notice or hearing even though he had traced his name to the 2002 voter lists. He speculated it was most likely because one of his documents had a period after Md while the other did not, and the software may have flagged that as a discrepancy. His appeal has been pending in the appellate tribunal since April 2026, even though his parents and siblings are included in the final voter rolls. “This is a subversion of democracy,” he said. “If this can happen to me, then what about those who do not have a voice?” Facing Growing Scrutiny In September 2026, the Indian Express published a series of investigations documenting that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had made decisions regarding the SIR unilaterally, often over the objections of the other two commissioners. This included decisions to delete names, to add new voters, and to increasingly centralize the electoral roll database. This limited the authority of officers responsible for verifying and finalizing the voter lists, a departure from the decentralized electoral system that the commission has always presented as one of its strongest safeguards. The Election Commission responded by saying differences of views among staff are part of the normal operations of any institution. Petitions challenging the revision process and seeking Kumar’s removal are before the Supreme Court. Former Chief Election Commissioner SY Quraishi said the SIR was “illegal” and called for those responsible in the Election Commission to be “criminally prosecuted.” In October, a current Supreme Court judge called the exercise “intrinsically arbitrary,” while a former Supreme Court judge spoke of Election Commission’s “malfunction.” A judge in the Bombay High Court questioned the purpose of the SIR if citizens were being removed from the voter rolls. Former Indian diplomats and government officials demanded that the exercise be scrapped, saying that it undermined India’s commitment to universal adult suffrage and made a mockery of its democracy. In May, three UN human rights experts warned that the SIR may amount to the instrumentalization of state administrative machinery “for the purpose of political targeting of a religious minority.” Disproportionate Harm to Women, Marginalized Communities The Election Commission’s stated purpose for the SIR was to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out” and “no ineligible person is included.” Yet existing evidence indicates that large numbers of citizens, disproportionately those from the most marginalized communities, have been wrongly excluded. An analysis of the SIR data by the Hindu found that significantly more women than men have been deleted across the country. Nearly 60 percent of those deleted in Bihar were women. In West Bengal, women constituted over 60 percent of those deleted from the voter rolls and as many as 6 million were unable to vote in the state’s legislative elections. Women made up more than half of the deleted voters in 88 percent of the constituencies in the state and are heavily concentrated especially in areas populated by Muslims, the Scheduled Caste Matua community, and Scheduled Tribes. Issues such as a change in one’s last name, spelling, address, or the ability to map to parents or grandparents have disproportionately affected single women, widows, and those living in poverty. Being marked as “permanently shifted” because of relocation to their husband’s homes after marriage is one of the main reasons women voters have been disproportionately excluded. In the third and final phase of the SIR, the Election Commission stopped disclosing the gender of the voters flagged as suspicious. Several women’s groups wrote to the poll body raising concerns over the large-scale exclusion of women and gender minorities from the exercise. Members of religious minorities, especially Muslims, are particularly likely to be removed from rolls due to third-party objections and being flagged by electoral software for “logical discrepancies.” Documentation by the Kolkata-based Sabar Institute found significant disparities. For instance, Muslims make up 20 percent of the Bhabanipur constituency, while nearly 52 percent of names on the logical discrepancy list are Muslim. A 34-year-old Muslim man in West Bengal said that although his father was on the rolls and he met the mapping requirement, his name was placed “under adjudication” pending verification by judicial officers because he comes from a family with eight siblings, leading the software to flag his registration as containing “logical discrepancies.” However, several of his siblings were included in the lists. During his hearing on February 5, he submitted his Aadhaar card, PAN card issued by the income tax authorities, and voter card, yet his name was deleted three days later. He filed an online appeal on February 12, which remains pending. The process also does not account for people who are estranged from their families. This leaves lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) people who are cut off by relatives due to their sexual orientation or gender identity at particular risk of exclusion. Those with severed family relations may not be traced to a relative or have access to documents, such as birth certificates and school records, which families often hold. Several transgender people whose families have abandoned them could not be traced to a relative on the last intensive revision rolls, trans rights activists said. Transgender people who have updated their identity documents face a heightened risk of exclusion. A 2014 Supreme Court ruling recognized transgender people’s right to legal gender recognition, and some transgender people have since updated their records. As a result, older records may carry one name and gender, and newer ones another. The lack of any procedure to reconcile such document mismatches makes it difficult to prove identity, and government-issued transgender identity certificates are not among the documents accepted by election authorities. A 27-year-old Hindu transgender man in West Bengal found his name removed from the rolls after his parents, who were included, refused to give him their voter card details for mapping and deliberately misinformed the booth-level officer of his whereabouts. The officer refused to include his name without his parents’ signature because his other documents reflected his previous name and sex assigned at birth. “I tried contacting my parents after I left home to explain myself to them,” he said. “But they wanted me to leave my partner and marry a man.” Some people whose homes were arbitrarily demolished after authorities claimed the homes were illegal have also been removed from the electoral rolls. In Delhi, about 87 percent of voters were deleted in nine polling stations where homes were demolished, with booth-level officers classifying the displaced voters as “absent/untraceable.” Those displaced were unclear on what address to include on their voter forms. In October, the Delhi Election Commission said it would organize “special camps” for voters whose homes were razed, enabling them to be enrolled. However, these were not uniformly organized across the country. The cost of challenging a deletion, including lost earnings, can make it harder for people with limited incomes, including workers paid by the day living in poverty, to secure reinstatement on the electoral rolls, compounding the barriers they face. In contrast, the authorities have at times bypassed their own official mechanisms to simplify reinstatement of prominent politicians, government officials, and actors. For instance, a notice issued to the Delhi chief minister for a logical discrepancy was resolved within hours without an official hearing. Denial of Access to Government Services, Social Security, and Education In July, the Supreme Court said that SIR data could not be used by the authorities for other purposes. However, information about deleted voters is being used to halt passport renewals and deny access to social security programs, residency certificates for students, and scholarships to children in public schools. In Bihar, the BJP state government removed over 3 percent of names from the public distribution system for subsidized food rations after their names were deleted from the electoral rolls. In May and June, West Bengal authorities published notices saying deleted voters who had not filed appeals in the tribunal would not be eligible for subsidized food grains or direct cash transfers for women under the state’s Annapurna Yojana program, but Human Rights Watch found that even those who had filed appeals were being denied access. A 38-year-old woman in South 24 Parganas district said she had registered for the Annapurna Yojana program in June, had received assistance in July, but then it abruptly stopped. Her name had been deleted from the voter roll in March even though her three siblings were included. She said she appealed the decision, but the state stopped her cash transfers anyway. “I valued that money a lot,” she said. “I used to pay my daughter’s school fees with it.” Another woman, 25, from the same district said she could not register for the cash transfer program after local authorities told her she was ineligible because her appeal was still pending at the tribunal. She had mapped herself to her mother, who was included in the final rolls, but both she and her father were excluded. “Just because our names have been deleted can’t mean that we don’t get any government benefits,” she said. A 45-year-old tailor in West Bengal said his 14-year-old son was denied a government scholarship of 1,200 rupees (about US$13) because both he and his wife had been struck off the rolls. The scholarship is for students from religious minority backgrounds, and school authorities had made parental inclusion on the voter lists an eligibility requirement. “The scholarship was necessary for him,” the man said. The Calcutta High Court in July directed the authorities not to take any “coercive steps” and to continue distributing subsidized food rations and issue government documents to those deleted from the SIR. However, deleted voters have had to continue to go to court to challenge the authorities’ refusal to comply. A 37-year-old man whose appeal is still pending in the tribunal approached the court in April after local authorities refused to issue a residence certificate for him. The man had secured a place in a PhD program at a public university but needed the document to finalize his admission. Using SIR for Unlawful Expulsions In December 2025, Home Minister Amit Shah defended the SIR as a means to “detect, delete, deport” alleged “infiltrators.” However, the Supreme Court clarified in May 2026 that the SIR was not a citizenship test. Indian authorities have also explicitly stated that documents such as passport, voter cards, and Aadhaar are not proof of citizenship. However, a valid voter card is inevitably tied to citizenship because it is presumptively issued only to Indian citizens. Those whose names have been struck off the rolls face heightened suspicion of being undocumented immigrants, a serious consequence given the ongoing unlawful and forcible expulsions of ethnic Bengali Muslims to Bangladesh. Since May 2025, Indian authorities have unlawfully expelled ethnic Bengali Muslims to Bangladesh without due process. After the SIR process was completed, the BJP state government in West Bengal set up detention camps in May 2026 under the “detect, delete, deport” policy and continued arbitrary detentions. In September, police in West Bengal attempted to detain a woman in Bankura district after her name was deleted from voter rolls. “The police said they had been ordered to detain people whose names were excluded from the SIR,” her lawyer said. “They called her an illegal migrant.” Her appeal has been pending in the tribunal since April. A 26-year-old queer Muslim woman in West Bengal’s Hooghly district said that landlords turned down her request to rent apartments and at least three organizations had rejected her job applications because her name was deleted from voter lists. “I feel scared,” she said, “What if they send me to Bangladesh just because my name is not on the voter list?”

items.title: Cameroun: au procès Martinez Zogo, le témoin Ayissi Nanga face aux questions de la partie civile
items.description: Après trois jours d'audience, le lieutenant-colonel Parfait Ayissi Nanga maintient que ce ne sont pas les coupables qui sont jugés devant le tribunal militaire. Durant leur contre-interrogatoire ce mercredi 28 octobre, les avocats de la partie civile ont tenté de relever des incohérences dans le discours de l'ancien membre de la commission mixte d'enquête. Ils ont également mis l'accent sur une forme d'acharnement du témoin envers sa hiérarchie et ont questionné son obstination à enquêter malgré son exclusion de la commission mixte.

items.title: Bobo-Dioulasso : Une dizaine d’élèves et d’étudiants interpellés lors d’une opération coup de poing
items.description: Ce mercredi 28 octobre 2026, la Police municipale de Bobo-Dioulasso, par l'intermédiaire de la Direction de la police de la salubrité et de la tranquillité urbaine (DPSTU), a déployé une opération ciblée contre la consommation de chicha et de boissons à forte teneur en alcool. Menée dans le cadre de la protection de la jeunesse et de la préservation de l'ordre public, cette descente sur le terrain a conduit à l'interpellation d'une dizaine d'élèves et d'étudiants. À travers cette action, l'institution municipale réaffirme sa vocation de force de proximité engagée pour la sécurité, la santé et la tranquillité des citoyens. La Police municipale de Bobo-Dioulasso intensifie ses contrôles sur le terrain. Ce mercredi 28 octobre 2026, les agents de la Direction de la police de la salubrité et de la tranquillité urbaine (DPSTU) ont mené une opération d'envergure visant à réprimer la consommation de chicha et de boissons à forte teneur en alcool. Cette intervention s'inscrit dans une dynamique globale de préservation du cadre de vie et de lutte contre les comportements dangereux au sein de la commune. Le bilan de cette descente met en lumière la vulnérabilité des milieux scolaires et universitaires face aux produits toxiques. Au cours des contrôles exécutés par les éléments de la DPSTU, une dizaine de jeunes — comprenant des élèves et des étudiants — ont été pris en infraction et interpellés. En ciblant l'usage de la chicha et des alcools forts, les forces de sécurité entendent poser un coup d'arrêt à des pratiques préjudiciables à la santé, au cursus scolaire et à l'avenir de la jeunesse locale. Au-delà du volet répressif, cette opération réaffirme un engagement fort pour la prévention et l'ordre public. À travers cette action, la Police municipale démontre sa volonté de protéger la jeunesse contre les fléaux de l'addiction tout en garantissant la quiétude dans les quartiers de la ville. Se positionnant comme une force de sécurité de proximité au service de la population, la municipalité entend maintenir la pression pour offrir un environnement sain et sécurisé à l'ensemble des Bobolais. L’article Bobo-Dioulasso : Une dizaine d'élèves et d'étudiants interpellés lors d'une opération coup de poing est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Commodity prices to surge 23pc, warns World Bank
items.description: WASHINGTON: Global commodity prices are set to surge 23 per cent in 2026, the World Bank said on Wednesday, citing rising energy prices and disruptions to cargo shipping during the Middle East war, grain shipment problems in the Black Sea and high demand for safe-haven assets such as gold. Oil, natural gas, food and metals prices all rose sharply this year as global shocks mounted, the World Bank said in its latest Commodity Markets Outlook. It said the situation could worsen if the conflict in the Middle East ratcheted up and damage to Russian oil infrastructure continued. Commodity prices were expected to ease by 7pc next year, it said, but continued shocks — including forecasts for the worst El Nino weather effect since 1950 — could keep food commodity prices elevated, raising the spectre of higher inflation and tighter monetary policy. The global economy was more vulnerable to future supply shocks at the moment. Global oil stocks have been depleted during the war in the Middle East, and global oil supply is expected to drop 5.2% in 2026, the biggest drop in four decades outside the 2020 global recession, the bank said. Energy up 32pc, metals 25pc, gold 40pc in 2026; food prices face El Nino threat “Commodity markets are being hit by several major shocks at once,” said Ayhan Kose, the World Bank’s deputy chief economist. “Higher energy costs and trade disruptions are driving up prices across a broad range of commodities, threatening to worsen inflation, food insecurity, and economic growth.” The bank released its twice-yearly report on Wednesday, two days before foreign ministers from the world’s 20 largest economies are due to gather in Atlanta, Georgia for a meeting that will focus on the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. Kose said the World Bank was focused on protecting the world’s poorest people and supporting low-income countries alrea­­dy grappling with heavy debt burdens. The bank had already provided $8.7 billion in low-cost loans and other aid to 25 countries affected negatively by the war in the Middle East, the report said. This included 10 countries that retooled existing programs to cover crisis-related expenses, and 19 that had tapped new resources, with some using both. The report, released twice a year, said global energy prices surged 32pc in 2026, reaching their highest level since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. With oil output down, Brent oil prices were expected to remain elevated in the near term, averaging $92 per barrel for the year. Prices would be even higher if oil demand were not forecast to drop 2.5pc this year, the third-largest drop behind the 2020 Covid shock and the 1980 oil crisis. It said food commodity prices were set to rise just over 10pc in 2026 due to grain shipment disruptions caused by hostilities between Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea, and another 7pc plus in 2027, for a cumulative increase of nearly 18pc. An adverse scenario that coupled a record El Nino, more Black Sea grain shipment disruptions, escalation in the Middle East conflict and ongoing damage to Russian oil infrastructure could drive food prices 12pc higher than expected, it said. That could trigger a food crisis like the one seen in the early 2010s, when more than 40 million additional people were pushed into extreme poverty, the bank noted. Fertiliser prices were expected to rise 14pc in 2026 due to a surge in urea prices, then return to 2025 levels in 2027. Metals prices were projected to rise 25pc and hit a new high in 2026, with aluminium, copper and tin all setting new records as a result of supply disruptions and strong demand from investments in renewable energy, electric vehicles and data centres, the bank said. Precious metals prices were projected to surge by 40pc in 2026, amid elevated demand for safe-haven assets triggered by geopolitical and policy uncertainty, with some moderation seen in 2027. Published in Dawn, October 29th, 2026

items.title: Mali: chasseurs dozos et jihadistes s'affrontent pour un village près de Djenné
items.description: Au Mali, le village de Sounga, qui appartient à la commune de Mougna, près de Djenné dans la région de Mopti, continue de résister aux jihadistes du Jnim, liés à al-Qaïda. Alors que les villages alentour se sont pliés à la domination des jihadistes, Sounga refuse de se soumettre, provoquant de violents affrontements la semaine dernière entre les jihadistes du Jnim et les chasseurs traditionnels dozos, qui s'efforcent de protéger les populations dans cette partie du territoire où l'armée malienne n'est pas présente.

items.title: Gaoua : Furieux de voir sa femme partir avec un rival, il incendie sa maison et le menace de mort
items.description: Condamné en première instance à sept ans de prison, dont quatre ans ferme, un planteur a vu sa peine réduite à trois ans d’emprisonnement, dont deux ans ferme, par la Cour d’appel de Bobo-Dioulasso, le lundi 26 octobre 2026. Il était poursuivi pour destruction volontaire de biens immeubles, port illégal d’arme à feu et menaces de mort, sur fond de rivalité amoureuse. Le Tribunal de grande instance (TGI) de Gaoua avait rendu son verdict le 24 mars 2026 dans cette affaire. Un planteur, identifié sous le nom d’emprunt de Kader, était poursuivi pour port illégal d’arme à feu, destruction volontaire de biens immeubles et menaces de mort. À l’issue du procès, il avait été reconnu coupable des faits qui lui étaient reprochés et condamné à sept ans d’emprisonnement, dont quatre ans ferme, ainsi qu’à une amende de 1 000 000 FCFA avec sursis. Il avait également été condamné à verser respectivement 950 000 FCFA et 850 000 FCFA aux parties civiles à titre de dommages et intérêts. Le 30 mars 2026, Kader a interjeté appel de cette décision, sollicitant une réduction de sa peine. Le lundi 26 octobre 2026, il a comparu devant la chambre correctionnelle de la Cour d’appel de Bobo-Dioulasso, à l’occasion d’une audience foraine, afin de répondre à nouveau des faits qui lui étaient reprochés. Une rivalité amoureuse à l’origine des faits Selon les éléments de l’enquête, Kader, planteur de profession, séjournait en Côte d’Ivoire avec son épouse pour des travaux champêtres. Lorsque cette dernière est tombée malade, il aurait décidé de la renvoyer dans leur village afin qu’elle puisse y recevoir des soins. De retour au village, la femme se serait retrouvée seule au domicile conjugal, sans nouvelles de son mari, resté en Côte d’Ivoire pendant une longue période. Au fil du temps, elle aurait fait la connaissance de Boubacar, un autre habitant du village, qui lui aurait proposé le mariage. Leur relation aurait évolué favorablement jusqu’au moment où la femme aurait quitté le domicile conjugal pour s’installer chez son nouveau compagnon. Quelques mois plus tard, Kader est rentré de Côte d’Ivoire. Il a alors découvert que son épouse vivait désormais avec Boubacar, qui envisageait de l’épouser. Selon les éléments du dossier, le projet de mariage avait été retardé à la demande des parents de la femme, qui avaient invité Boubacar à patienter. Face à cette situation, Kader aurait tenté de rencontrer son rival pour trouver une solution à l’amiable. Mais, selon les déclarations rapportées au dossier, Boubacar n’aurait pas souhaité renoncer à son projet de mariage, estimant que la femme n’avait jamais été mariée auparavant. Choqué et sous l’effet de la colère, Kader aurait alors décidé de se faire justice lui-même. Des supplications restées vaines Dans un premier temps, Kader aurait sommé Boubacar de quitter le village. Il se serait ensuite rendu à son domicile. Ne trouvant pas son rival sur place, il aurait interrogé la cousine de ce dernier, Aïcha, qui lui aurait expliqué que son cousin était sorti. C’est alors que Kader aurait sorti un briquet et mis le feu à la maison. Aïcha aurait tenté de le raisonner, lui faisant comprendre que le différend concernait son cousin et non elle. Mais ses supplications seraient restées vaines. Selon les faits rapportés dans le dossier, Kader aurait ensuite sorti un fusil de calibre 12 et tiré plusieurs coups de feu en l’air. Il aurait également menacé de tuer Aïcha. Lors de l’audience de première instance, le prévenu aurait tenu des propos laissant entendre que son rival devrait quitter le village à sa sortie de prison, faute de quoi il partirait lui-même. Ces déclarations avaient notamment suscité des interrogations sur ses intentions. Le président du tribunal lui avait alors demandé qui était la femme au centre de cette rivalité. Il ressortait des débats que celle-ci était sa cousine. Interrogé sur les pratiques matrimoniales au sein de sa famille, Kader avait répondu par l’affirmative. Le ministère public lui avait ensuite demandé ce qu’il entendait par ses propos concernant le départ de son rival ou le sien. Le prévenu n’avait pas souhaité répondre à cette question. La défense invoque la colère Prenant la parole, le conseil de Kader a plaidé en faveur de son client, estimant que celui-ci avait agi sous l’effet de la colère. Selon l’avocat, peu d’hommes auraient su garder leur sang-froid dans une situation comparable. Il a estimé que son client avait fait preuve de retenue et aurait pu perdre davantage le contrôle de lui-même. Le conseil a également soutenu que son client avait retrouvé ses esprits et regrettait les propos qu’il avait tenus à l’encontre de son rival. Il a ainsi plaidé pour une certaine clémence de la Cour. Le parquet demande le maintien de la peine Dans ses réquisitions, le ministère public a estimé que la décision rendue en première instance était justifiée et ne devait pas être révisée à la baisse. Pour le parquet, les faits étaient caractérisés et le prévenu les avait reconnus. Il a considéré que la peine prononcée était déjà appropriée au regard de la gravité des faits. En conséquence, le ministère public a demandé à la Cour de maintenir la condamnation initiale, soit sept ans d’emprisonnement, dont quatre ans ferme, ainsi qu’une amende de 1 000 000 FCFA avec sursis. Une peine réduite en appel Après la suspension de l’audience et le délibéré, la Cour d’appel a finalement déclaré Kader coupable des faits de destruction volontaire de biens immeubles, de port illégal d’arme à feu et de menaces de mort. Toutefois, contrairement aux réquisitions du ministère public, la Cour a réduit sa peine à 36 mois d’emprisonnement, dont 24 mois ferme, assortis d’une amende de 1 000 000 FCFA avec sursis. Le prévenu reste également tenu de verser les sommes de 950 000 FCFA et de 850 000 FCFA aux victimes, à titre de dommages et intérêts. items.title: Drame de la route à Léo : Le Parquet lance un appel à témoins après la mort tragique de l’élève Dorcas Sanou
items.description: À la suite de l'accident mortel de la circulation ayant coûté la vie à l'élève Dorcas Sanou le samedi 10 octobre 2026 sur la RN 06 à Léo, le Procureur du Faso près le Tribunal de grande instance (TGI) de Léo, Ahmed Ouattara, a diffusé un communiqué officiel d'appel à témoins ce mercredi 28 octobre 2026. Bien qu'un suspect soit désormais appréhendé et poursuivi pour homicide involontaire, défaut de maîtrise et délit de fuite, le Parquet sollicite la collaboration active des populations de la province de la Sissili. L'objectif est de collecter tout élément matériel témoignages, clichés, enregistrements ou indices d'immatriculation susceptible d'éclairer la vérité lors des futurs débats judiciaires. L'émotion demeure vive au sein des habitants de Léo et de la communauté scolaire de la province. Le samedi 10 octobre 2026, la jeune élève Sanou Dorcas a perdu la vie dans un tragique accident de la circulation routière survenu au niveau du secteur n°03 de Léo, sur la Route nationale 06 (RN 06), précisément en face de la pharmacie Sissili. L'accident, d'une grande brutalité, impliquait un camion dont le conducteur avait immédiatement pris la fuite, abandonnant la victime sur la chaussée. Dès la survenue du drame, une enquête judiciaire a été ouverte sous la direction du Parquet du Procureur du Faso. Grâce aux premières investigations menées par les services de sécurité, les enquêteurs sont parvenus à identifier et interpeller un suspect. Ce dernier fait aujourd'hui l'objet de poursuites pénales pour défaut de maîtrise, homicide involontaire et délit de fuite. Cependant, pour le Parquet de Léo, l'arrestation du présumé responsable ne constitue qu'une étape. Afin de garantir un procès équitable et rigoureux, l'autorité judiciaire estime indispensable de réunir l'ensemble des preuves matérielles et des témoignages directs pour établir précisément le déroulement des faits. C'est tout le sens du communiqué officiel n° 640_2026/CAO/TGI-L/PF signé le 28 octobre 2026 par le magistrat Ahmed Ouattara, Procureur du Faso près le TGI de Léo. Le Parquet invite instamment toute personne ayant assisté de près ou de loin à l'accident, ou détenant des éléments pertinents — tels que des photographies, des enregistrements, des détails sur le véhicule ou son numéro d'immatriculation —, à se manifester dans les plus brefs délais. Les citoyens disposant d'informations peuvent se rendre au Commissariat central de police de Léo, au Secrétariat du Parquet près le TGI de Léo, ou joindre directement les services judiciaires au 25 41 62 52. Comptant sur le sens civique de la population, la justice entend ainsi honorer la mémoire de la jeune élève et apporter des réponses incontestables à sa famille.
